Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a statement to the House on the subject of colour television. Hon. Members know that this is a matter of growing importance and concern to Canadians in view of the rapid
development of colour transmissions in the United States.
There is now clear evidence that an important part of the combined total output of the three largest American broadcasting networks will henceforth be in colour, and the rapid rise of colour set acquisitions in the United States indicates that a definite shift has taken place in that country from black and white to colour television.
Better than 50 per cent of Canadian homes with television sets are within reach of direct television signals from the United States, so that a situation is rapidly developing in Canada not unlike that of 1951-52, just prior to the commencement of Canadian television, when a large audience developed in Canada for direct American television broadcasts.
The Government has asked the Committee on Broadcasting to examine this matter and report on the situation. I reported to the House last week that the conclusions of the Committee on Broadcasting, because of the complexities of the study, cannot be available until late in the summer. I regret this, but I repeat that the subject matter of the study is indeed important and complex so that the delays were perhaps to be expected. However, the Government now finds it necessary to make a clear statement on colour television in advance of the Broadcast Committee report.
There are several reasons for this. First, it is necessary to give guidance to the Canadian electronics industry and to the broadcasters in Canada on the technical standards which will be adopted. Second, it is necessary to announce a firm commencement date for colour television in Canada so the telecommunications and broadcasting industries can work together on their plans. Third, it is necessary to authorize the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to instal colour television equipment in the facilities which will be made available for the various countries participating in Expo '67.
The advice given to the Government by the broadcasters and the electronics industry is that up to 18 months notice must be given in advance of the commencement of colour television service so the complex engineering work and the various facilities installations can be completed.
2408	COMMONS DEBATES	June 15, 1965
Colour Television Service
The Government has decided that the transmission of colour programs from Expo in 1967 is a necessity since three or four other countries have already indicated their intention and desire to make such colour transmissions, notably the United States, Japan, Great Britain and possibly France. There may be others also since many other countries seem now to be planning for colour television within the next two years.
If there is to be a colour television service in Canada on April 1, 1967 it will be seen that the time for decision is upon us. Both the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the private broadcasters must be given the same advance notice and permission to proceed.
We are advised by the Committee on Broadcasting that they will recommend the commencement of colour television in Canada in 1967. They will also recommend proceeding with caution, since the implementation of colour will be a costly addition to the broadcasting budget in Canada, but that it is inevitable because of the United States colour programs.
It will, of course, be necessary for the Government to consider the cost factor very carefully, and to ensure that higher priorities, such as the extension of broadcast coverage and the necessity for improved Canadian programming, are not lost sight of.
In conclusion therefore, Mr. Speaker, I am announcing the intention of the Government, through my colleague the Minister of Transport, to prescribe the colour television standards to be applied in Canada. I am announcing also the willingness of the Government to permit the immediate application by broadcasters, under the Radio Act, for licenses for colour transmissions to commence not earlier than January 1, 1967. Finally, I am announcing the intention of the Government to authorize the C.B.C. to proceed with the necessary contractual arrangement for the installation of colour television equipment at Expo' 67 and, since the C.B.C. national English and French networks must carry these signals, the preparation of the necessary alterations to the transmitters and network facilities of the C.B.C. for this purpose. These arrangements are, of course, subject to the approval of further funds by Parliament for this purpose.
The further plans of the C.B.C. for colour should await the Broadcasting Committee report, and as I have already stated the Government will study carefully the whole

question of broadcasting priorities before making further recommendations to the House.
Eight Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition): I think in this case the Government has adopted a most unusual way of making a decision in respect of something of paramount importance to Canada and Canadians. We have endeavoured over and over again to bring together the House committee on broadcasting to discuss this and other matters connected with broadcasting, but without success. In every case when the need for expanding the present facilities in those areas which are now denied television has been pointed out the answer has been that nothing can be done in that connection until the Fowler Committee reports. On several occasions the hon. Member for Churchill has brought before the Government the question of the areas he represents, only to be met by a stone wall,-with statements that no action can be taken until the advisory committee makes its report.
Now suddenly the Government finds itself announcing policy with regard to broadcasting and, in particular, with regard to colour broadcasting, because of Expo '67. It is most laudable to have all the facilities available. After all we are to have a $10 million broadcasting building, and there has to be something to broadcast from the exhibition. This, apparently, is a step taken to justify the expenditure of the $10 million which, to my way of thinking, was a completely unnecessary and wasteful expenditure. I think the time has come to look into the expenditures of Expo '67 in so far as federal responsibility is concerned.
To return to the question of colour television, certainly this is a step all of us have looked forward to, but the manner in which the Government has gone about it indicates the haphazard thinking of those who sit opposite. A few weeks ago nothing could be done until the committee had reported. Now the committee has been communicated with to find out what its recommendation will be before they make it. Did you ever hear of a proposition like that? Why can we not find out what are the other recommendations the committee intends to make? Why the unearthly haste in this regard? Necessary as colour broadcasting is in the light of the advances which are taking place, the explanation given by the Minister simply indicates that this is another step in the way of Canada's policy being determined by what is necessary for Expo '67.
June 15, 1965	COMMONS
It seems to me strange to anticipate what the committee will do in advance of the report, when all over this country there are areas that are without ordinary television, and when advances in new colour television technology and broadcasting are apparently taking place in the United States. This is just another example of the kind of evasion this Government adopts toward the Parliament of Canada.
We have asked for the House committee on broadcasting to he convened, hut we have been met by arrogant indifference and cavalier disregard for the rights of Parliament, the explanation being simply that the Government cannot do this because it has set up a group of individuals outside of Parliament and must wait for their recommendations. We now are asked to accept this kind of policy placed before us haphazardly with complete disregard for the rights of Parliament.
I welcome any action that may be taken in respect of colour television in Canada, but at the same time I say that the manner of going about this indicates the uncertainty with which this Government faces the problems of the nation.

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Official Opposition might have mentioned another point about the Committee on Broadcasting which I think is even more bizarre, and that is that one of the key members of that trio is the Minster's own Deputy Minister. We have the very odd situation now of a committee recommending policy to the Government, one of whose members is the Minister's main adviser. This is certainly one of the most intriguing approaches to Government policy matters that I have encountered.
I mention this point because it just seems stupid that such major decisions affecting expenditures by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on such a scale are revealed to us in this way without any preliminaries at all. I wonder what kind of a committee this Committee on Broadcasting really is, in view of the fact that it has been unable to produce a report up to this time. What will be the situation if the report is projected into the future and we only have a partial tip-off?
I think it is time we knew just what duties the three members of the Broadcasting Committee are carrying out in addition to their committee work. Is Mr. Fowler still doing a considerable amount of work for the Canadian Pulp and Paper Association? Is
DEBATES	2409
Colour Television Service Mr. Lalonde still active in his legal practice, for instance, in connection with the Royal Commission on Pilotage? Is Mr. Steele, the Deputy Minister, still trying to carry a full load of departmental duties? It seems to me these are questions that need to be answered.
The Minister, I suppose anticipating a certain amount of criticism, did drag in two points that are objectionable in connection with this plan. He mentioned that the policy on the extension of television services is still incomplete. The Government has been asked about this for several years, and the C.B.C. gave a figure of $20 million in respect of the capital investment necessary to complete this program. In the meantime we are to get all this fancy stuff for Expo '67. We also have that wonderful radio station in Toronto broadcasting in French to no one or almost no one. We have also been told about the future plans for expansion all across the country-
Shame.

My hon. friends cry "Shame". I have no objection to broadcasting of this kind, but I think there should be an audience before these expenditures are made.
The point I really want to make in relation to this announcement is that the Minister has opened up almost a Pandora's box of expenditures by the C.B.C. in preparation, yet we have not even received an undertaking from the Minister that the estimates of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will be placed before the committee at an early date. It just seems to me that the whole approach reflects inadequate planning.
The last point I want to make is that there is no question in my mind but that the introduction of colour television in this country will be popular. In this sense I welcome the announcement of the date and also the idea of our manufacturers being able to enter into the production of sets knowing a market is ahead of them. This will enable them to bring down the cost of such sets, which at the present time is very high.
Having said that, it certainly does not excuse the way the Committee on Broadcasting has been allowed to dawdle along in view of the carte blanche which has been given the C.B.C, in terms of expenditures on which we have no check or projection. All we have is this interesting announcement.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think anyone is going to object to the prospect of having colour television in Canada. After all, countries like
2410	COMMONS
Colour Television Service Japan have had several colour television networks for a number of years. We at least ought to be moving into this area by the time of our centennial. Therefore we approve the announcement from that standpoint.
However, I must join with those who have already spoken in criticizing the method by which this decision has been made. Surely the announcement is extremely unusual. How is it that other important matters involving broadcasting must wait until the Fowler Commission report is in, yet this particular aspect of broadcasting can move ahead without any question at all?
Another very important matter in this regard is this. How is it that we in this House are committed to the expenditure of millions of dollars to bring about colour television without even having had the privilege of considering the subject in committee? Therefore we must join in the protests which have been made in view of the fact that apparently this is not the normal procedure. I ask what is the reason behind this action.
Another interesting thing is that only yesterday it was announced by the C.B.C. that there would be a director of overseas and foreign relations. I would ask what that means. Does it mean we are going to step up our program of foreign broadcasting? Does it mean we will use some of the excellent programs which are available? Does it means still more expenditure without consultation with this House through a committee on broadcasting? Surely this whole matter should have been referred to a committee on broadcasting if it could not wait until the Fowler Commission report was presented. I think there are real grounds for protest in the strongest way of this very unusual action which has been announced today.

Mr. Speaker,
I would be the last to criticize the statement made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) to the effect that Canada will at long last have colour television. On the contrary, notwithstanding the manner in which he made that statement, I believe that he deserves congratulations. This is an era of progress, and in the field of television as well as in other areas Canada should join modern times and have colour television. That is why I am happy to congratulate the Secretary of State for the announcement he just made today, and I hope that this will be an unprecedented success.

Mr. Speaker, this bill seeks to expand the criminal libel sections of the Criminal Code to include hate literature, which is sometimes referred to as group defamatory libel. It would make it an offence

Inquiries of the Ministry for any group to be held up to hatred, contempt or ridicule because of racial, religious or national background. In addition it would give the officer trying such a case discretion to send an accused for mental observation for 30 days if that presiding officer should see fit to do so. Mr. Speaker, as my right hon. friend knows, the channel of communication in such matters would be from one government to another. If one body having legislative authority in a

province takes a position involving a matter such as is purported in the telegram to which my right hon. friend refers, the communication to the Government of Canada would have to come through the proper channel, which in this instance must be the Government of the Province of Quebec. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister of Justice a question which I put to his Parliamentary Secretary yesterday, reminding him that on February 23 he told the House he would try to make an announcement on the Government's policy with regard to parole prior to the date on which the House votes on capital punishment. Has he enunciated a new policy, or does he still expect to make the announcement prior to that important vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PROPOSED CHANGES IN PAROLE SYSTEM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I considered this matter after my Parliamentary Secretary referred the question to me. In reconsidering the question in the light of the fact that the matter of capital punishment is to be submitted to the House to be decided by a free vote, I think it would be more proper for me not to make any assumption as to what that vote eventually will be, so as not to prejudice the question in any way. But for the information of the House I may recall that some months ago the Government amended the parole regulations to provide that in the case of a person whose death sentence has been commuted to life imprisonment, he may not be paroled except after study of his case and leave being given by the Government.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PROPOSED CHANGES IN PAROLE SYSTEM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, with the uncertainty that prevails as to what the House may do in a free vote on the matter of the abolition of capital punishment, may I ask the Minister if it is the intention of the Government, until the vote takes place, to withhold any executions that are ordered or directed? I think that is the course that is generally followed when a matter of this nature is to be brought before Parliament. I am simply asking for information.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PROPOSED CHANGES IN PAROLE SYSTEM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think this question has already been answered in the House. The announcement which has already been made is to the effect that pending any change in the law, or any confirmation of the law as it presently stands, each case as it comes up will be considered on its own merits.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PROPOSED CHANGES IN PAROLE SYSTEM

speechtext:
Yesterday 1 undertook to complete my answer to the question put to me by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North having reference to the Commissioner of the R.C.M.P. being quoted in the Telegram recently as saying that the R.C.M.P. teaches its staff methods of electronic intrusion techniques.
I have been assured by the Commissioner that this was mentioned not in relation to the use or intended use of such methods and devices by R.C.M.P. members, but exclusively in relation to the knowledge which members of the R.C.M.P. must have of modern techniques used by professional criminals or by agents involved in subversive activities so they may be better able to counteract them.

Last month, you may recall, the Minister of Finance, after having disingenuously as I described it as kindly as possible, reiterated a misapprehension which he had at first including some astronomical figure which flowed from it in respect of my amendment- I may say that he did so twice in the space of five minutes-finally made what on the surface might be considered a legitimate objection to the amendment. This charge of sloppy draftsmanship or, what is even worse, a rather sloppy approach to this question strikes me as being rather interesting, because this is the Minister who told us on April 26, 1965, when he was introducing an amendment to ensure that contributions to the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec pension plan would be fully deductible in calculating taxable income-I am sorry the Minister finds it necessary to leave but I will not allow his absence to inhibit me in what I have to say, as I am sure you, Sir, will convey my comments to him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should just like to assure the hon. Member that the Minister will return very shortly.

If what I suggested was the Minister's purpose, then it seems to me this particular budget resolution he presented on April 26 is a masterpiece of sloppy draftsmanship. Certainly those individuals in the lower income brackets will receive compensation for their contributions to pension plans, but only just enough to pay for those contributions. They would have to reach an income of some $6,800 before they could draw more in tax abatements than they pay in pension plan contributions. Let us take as an example a taxpayer with an income of $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000, or one who has reached the limit of his tax abatement of $600. In the wisdom of the Government and Parliament only individuals with incomes between $600 and $5,000 are subject to contri-
Income Tax Act
butions to the pension plan. What happens if a taxpayer has an income which is high enough to enable him to collect the maximum of $600 in the way of tax abatement? We find that he is to be given a bonus of either $520.80 or $441.60 per year, depending upon whether he is employed or self employed, is paying the whole contribution or only the employer's portion. That individual will receive this extra bonus in order that the lower income groups may be fully compensated for their payments to the pension plan. If that is not an example of sloppy draftsmanship I do not know what is.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, our Minister of Finance and his advisers are not so incompetent that they had to arrange matters so that those individuals in the upper income brackets would receive bonuses to the extent I have mentioned in order that individuals in lower income brackets may be assured that they will have their pension plan payments covered by tax rebates. I suspect that this was done because it was the easiest thing to do. I suspect it was done because it was much easier to pluck the 10 per cent figure out of the air and spread it all across the board than to revise the income tax structure.
What the Minister proposes-that is, to ensure that those individuals in the lower income bracket will have their pension plan payments covered or compensated for by the income tax rebate-is good, but I think it ill becomes the Minister of Finance to chide me for carelessness in the drafting of an amendment which is obviously a very short and simple submission to the House, without an elaborate explanation of the revisions that would be required in respect of income brackets above the level proposed, in view of the fact that he has produced legislation of this sort which will have the result of paying bonuses to people in an income bracket sufficiently high to enable them to receive the total $600 rebate. The bonuses payable will be, as I have said, $520.80 or $441.60, and are designed to ensure that individuals in the lower income brackets will be compensated. That to my mind is careless and lazy drafting, in respect of which the Minister should be severely criticized and reprimanded.
There is another matter covered by this budget resolution to which I should like to direct some comments, and I refer to that portion which deals with advertising in newspapers. I think all of us will have some sympathy with the Minister in his attempts to

Income Tax Act
encourage the development and expansion of Canadian publications, and I presume that is the purpose of this legislation. I assume that he is attempting to offset the very large extent to which foreign advertisement now influences the Canadian reader. But I am wondering whether the Minister has thought of the possible consequence of his attempt to curb advertising by Canadian advertisers in foreign newspapers and periodicals. Has it occurred to him that the result may well be not to increase advertising by Canadian advertisers in Canadian publications but possibly merely to divert this advertising to United States television and radio stations.
I suggest that in my Province there is a striking example of this at the present time. The television station at Bellingham serves to a great extent the large Vancouver metropolitan market rather than the United States centre. At the present time many Canadian advertisers take advantage of the services provided by the television station at Bellingham, and I think this sort of thing is likely to be the result of the Minister's very worthy attempts to safeguard the position of Canadian publishers of Canadian newspapers.
This brings me to another aspect of the problem, Mr. Chairman, and I hope you will be lenient with me because although it is not actually covered in these resolutions, it is related to them. The purpose of the Minister's resolution seems to be to protect and encourage the development of Canadian publications. If that is so then I think we must consider the position of these phony Canadian editions of United States publications. I have in mind two in particular, Time magazine and Reader's Digest, both of which in addition to being United States publications masquerading as Canadian publications are intrinsically vicious elements in our public media in Canada. Time magazine is tendentious, to say the least. Reader's Digest is composed, as everyone knows, of planted articles, which is the very lowest type of journalism. These two publishing firms have been allowed to set up in Canada so-called Canadian editions, which I understand are printed in Canada but the entire editorial content of which comes from New York, across the line. These two magazines come here, of course, for one purpose or one principal purpose, which is to take advantage of the very generous postal regulations in Canada with regard to periodicals.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I suggest to the Minister of Finance that if he is really concerned with protecting

Canadian publications and promoting their development he should take appropriate steps to redefine in very careful terms what constitutes a Canadian publication, in such a way as to exclude these extremely dubious publications which now masquerade as Canadian periodicals. I imagine this would entail some regulations under the Post Office Act. It might even entail some tariff revisions to keep out the editorial matter coming from New York; I am not sure of that. But I am sure the Minister, his colleagues and his staff could work out something which would prevent Time magazine and Reader's Digest from shamelessly taking advantage of the very generous provisions which we make in Canada regarding postage for periodicals.
I have always regretted, Mr. Chairman, that the provisions of the O'Leary Commission report in this regard were not carried out. I think it is idle for the Minister of Finance to imagine that he is doing anything substantial to protect our Canadian identity and to protect the position of Canadian periodicals merely by bringing in this amendment to the taxation act. It will penalize Canadian advertisers who advertise in United States publications, advertising which, according to the text of the resolution, is primarily designed for the Canadian market.
Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, this brings to mind another point. I am not quite clear how the Minister is going to decide where this advertising is directed. How is he going to determine whether it is directed to the citizens of Toronto or the citizens of Buffalo? Obviously the appeal will be made to both groups in the same manner. I suspect that this will become almost a dead letter. On the other hand, if the Minister and his colleagues will pluck up their courage and deal with these two very powerful publications and see that they are no longer allowed to masquerade as Canadian publications, then for the first time in all his commendable patriotic endeavours to protect the Canadian economy and Canadian identity he will have done something toward this end, instead of just going through the motions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I intend to confine myself to that portion of the resolution dealing with publications, and to look into the reason for and the genesis of this legislation, which in my opinion is a serious first step along the road to control of the press in Canada.
I realize there are many who feel that action should be taken to protect what is
June 15, 1965

called the Canadian identity. However, as one views this legislation one can only conclude that it has been put together most haphazardly, and that it will not achieve the purposes for which it is ostensibly intended. Indeed, an argument has just been made by the hon. Member who has just taken his seat to the effect that if it is brought into effect it can only mean that radio and television stations across the line which enjoy a tremendous influence in the border areas of our country, will become the main advertising media, and that advertising which would normally go to Canadians will join the exodus to the United States.
On the face of it I think this is dangerous legislation, dangerous in the degree to which it places in the hands of a government the power to control. A great deal of thought control has been practised by this Government during the past two years. One has but to listen to some of the broadcasts that take place and read some of the articles in the press to come to the conclusion that they have all the appearance of having been directed by the Government. Indeed, when matters which cause controversy arise in this House one can always be sure that the following day among the broadcasts over the C.B.C. will be those of commentators who explain away matters which are subject to criticism. I know it is only a coincidence, but when coincidence appears to be the regular course the ultimate conclusion is that there are other explanations than mere chance. So I say at once that in so far as this legislation is concerned it constitutes a major interference with basic principles which are inherent in the concept of freedom of the press.
This is a Government that is afraid of United States investment. This is a Government representing a party which two or three years ago was criticizing the Government of that day for being anti-American. Within a period of over two years the course taken by this Government has been antiAmerican, indeed to such an extent that it has become anti-Canadian. The Government is afraid of American investment, but it was not afraid to provide $50 million a year to the great United States automobile companies on the basis of the recent parts agreement.
Do I exaggerate the meaning of this legislation if it is implemented? Did the Canadian daily newspaper publishers talk foolishness and nonsense on May 4? This is foolishness and nonsense on the part of the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister and possibly the Minister of Justice. The Daily Newspaper 22620-155
Income Tax Act
Publishers Association said this proposal "is a fundamental violation of long established press freedom".
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Several of those who made that statement have been avowed supporters of the Government of the day. They asked the Government to drop this legislation. I ask them now, on behalf of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, to drop it. This legislation is dangerous. It may not seem dangerous to those who would like to control the thinking of the people of the country, but this legislation places newspapers in all parts of Canada in a position where a first step has been taken to throttle freedom of expression. Again I point out the Daily Newspaper Publishers Association said the measure involves a fundamental violation of long established press freedom in Canada.
When I speak on behalf of the freedom of the press, may I say no one has had that freedom used against him to a greater extent than I have during the past several years. Yet, having had that experience, I assert that the maintenance of freedom of the press as more important than anything else toward the assurance of freedom within the country. That does not interest the Minister of Finance. He has ideas. He has had ideas during the last two or three years which, to use a colloquial expression, were the most cockeyed ever presented in Parliament.
One disaster after another.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
He has had to withdraw most of them. He proposes and finally the Government as a whole disposes by dropping his most hoped for endeavours. The resolution said the publishers wished to record "our serious protest" against the budget proposal. It went on to say:
To employ in any degree or manner a tax restraint or incentive on advertising as a means of regulating the press of this country, or its ownership, is a fundamental violation of long established press freedom in Canada.
Who supported that? Were they political opponents, or were they people who understand freedom and its preservation? Among them were Mr. R. A. Graybiel, of the Windsor Star, Basil Dean of the Edmonton Journal, Aurele Gratton of Le Droit of Ottawa and R. S. Malone of F.P. Publications Limited. Mr. Graybiel reported that they had a good reception from the Prime Minister. It is not a good reception that is being asked; it is an end to this threatened legislation. This is what we want to achieve.

I am referring now to a Canadian Press dispatch in the Montreal Gazette of May 5, Mr. Graybiel was asked about the Minister's statement in the House that those opposing the proposed legislation should put forth alternatives, and in reply he said that the executive of their association "had not been empowered by its 103 member papers to make such proposals".
Alternatives are not needed. When a Government introduces a resolution such as this, which cannot but have the effect of hobbling freedom, alternatives are not needed. There is only one alternative to this legislation, and that is to withdraw it and get rid of it. The Minister will grow in importance in this country by taking such action. He will not be spoiling the record of the Government. It has the greatest long distance record of running away from its proposals and throwing them overboard of any government in history. Why spoil that record by adhering to something so questionable as this proposal?
I do not often read from editorials, but I intend to make a couple of references. The Toronto Globe and Mail had an editorial entitled "Useless-And Worse". I think the Globe and Mail is one of the admirers of the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Fredericton Gleaner says:
Another flaw has become apparent in the Government's budget proposal to refuse income tax credits for advertising. ..It is now rumoured that proposal may be a violation of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade to which Canada is a signatory.
Then it goes on to say how dangerous this legislation is. The Winnipeg Free Press had an editorial headed "Swelling Protests". They ask why the Minister did this. Why this solicitude for the newspapers? They did not ask for it. You know, Mr. Chairman, there are so many things that have been asked for, such as fairness for our old age pensioners, such as a new sense of responsibility toward the superannuated civil servants. These things have been asked for but the Government has not given them. This is something that has not been asked for by the newspapers of Canada. With reference to the resolution of the Canadian Daily Newspaper Publishers Association the Winnipeg Free Press had this to say:
The resolution also noted that, historically government influence on press freedom through taxation techniques "went on far longer and more insidiously in Great Britain than did direct censorship of news."
What that has to do with, of course, is the fact that in 1712 a stamp tax was imposed on newspapers at the rate of a penny a sheet, and by 1815 it had risen to fourpence a copy. The purpose was to restrain the abuses arising from the publication of blasphemous and seditious libels. But the action was dangerous; it interfered with freedom, and finally the tax was abolished in the 1850's. The proposal now before us brings back legislation that was abolished over 100 years ago in the United Kingdom as dangerous. The Free Press went on to say with regard to these controls:
They could lay open the way for some future and less scrupulous government to use them as a method of punishing or bestowing favours on Canadian newspapers.
The Free Press also had an editorial headed "Unwanted Protection" in which it said in part:
Whether by design or through sheer clumsiness, what the Minister proposes would give this and all future governments the power to Interfere with the right of all Canadians to read what they choose.
Nobody would say it was sheer clumsiness by this Government. The Winnipeg Free Press says that this measure strikes at the freedom of newspapers. It says also that the object, which is laudable enough, is to ensure that
June 15. 1965

essential communications media remain in the hands of Canadian citizens. The article goes on to point out the grave dangers to which these moves will lead.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I should quote from one of the greatest Canadians of our time, even though today he is living in the United Kingdom. I refer to Lord Thomson, Roy Thomson, a man whose life has been, for the most part, the embodiment of the Alger story, a man who in the operation of his vast empire of newspapers and periodicals has, as a Canadian, extended the field of public information to a degree never before known. He says this:
It Is in violation of the universal declaration of human rights of the United Nations, where Article 19 specifies that everyone has the right to freedom of information and expression, a right which includes freedom to hold opinions without interference and to seek, receive and impart information and ideas through any media.
The purpose is to prevent foreign corporations from actively controlling or directing Canadian thinking. Well, what about Time magazine? Read Time magazine week by week. As the hon. gentleman who preceded me said, it masquerades as Canadian but it has only four or six pages of Canadian news in the Canadian edition. Canadian? Read the articles, and read the degree to which, week by week, Time magazine views Canadian problems from the point of view of the Government of the day. Is the Government fearful of the control of Canadian thinking by another country? On the occasion when I visited Commonwealth countries, Mr. Chairman, I found one item in Time magazine during that entire trip which had to do with Canada, and it was in miscellany. Canada gets less attention than does a republic with a population of 300,000.
Then there is Reader's Digest, which established itself here. We should remember that these two magazines have 40 per cent of Canadian magazine advertising. It is a tremendous power to be used, if used to control Canadian thinking.
Well, from where did this all come? It did not come from the O'Leary report. The O'Leary report said nothing about newspapers. It dealt with two magazines and that is all. There was nothing about newspapers. What is wrong with advertising? What is the basis upon which this legislation has been introduced? Are we to have a mentally controlled electorate, determined in its decisions by the fear of what the Government can do? One of the vital needs of democracy is a free 22620-1551

press to keep the public fully informed with impartiality. The performance of this function, which is indispensable to freedom, requires that the freedom of the press be maintained. I am concerned with the philosophy of the bureaucrats behind this legislation. Eight of them sit over there, former top bureaucrats, and they like to cut through things. It is their viewpoint, I am sure, which in large measure is represented by the thinking behind this legislation.
I intend to quote from one of the leaders of Liberalism today, Mr. Tom Kent. Mr. Kent is a bureaucrat today who looks after the so-called war on poverty, the war on the poor. He is above Parliament. He enjoys a position of power about which even he had to smile when he was on private television and was asked questions by young men and women. He is the father of this. Sometimes it is difficult to find the putative father of some of these ideas that spring up from time to time, but not in this case. He was in Kingston in July, 1960. I have here a copy of his speech, which was one of the longest in history, 66 pages. Most people just measured it, but I read it. I want to set out these views which represent the philosophy of this individual today as he directs the policies that should be followed. His thesis is that Government direction of economic behaviour is necessary in order to expand social security, the redistribution of wealth.
Now, all of us believe in social security. How far did that gentleman go at the meeting to which I have referred? I think it is well to quote some of the expressions used, even though quotation is sometimes very tiring. I now read from page 61:
The business expenditures that are of great fiscal interest are those on advertising and merchandising generally. This is the major respect in which, because of the imperfection of competition and the distortion induced by taxation, the "hidden hand" is not working. The magnetism of the market is not inducing business as a whole to find its profit, as in theory it does, in what the community wants. Business is engaged now in a gigantic effort to tell the community what to want.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
That is his philosophy. He does not like advertising. It is not the kind of thing that should be done. Businesses should not develop and expand through advertising. It is bad for the people to consider buying what they think they would like to have. What we should have is a control over advertising so that people will only be able to buy that which the bureaucrats feel is good for them

to purchase. If you think I overstate it I shall read on:
Business is engaged now in a gigantic effort to tell the community what to want. In the process it wastes talent: it gives every possible encouragement to wage demands, excessive personal indebtedness, and inflationary forces generally, and by stimulating unimportant wants it increases the reluctance of people to satisfy their far more important collective wants, for schools and the rest.
Socialism at its worst never equalled Kent at his best. No wonder they sometimes say that the Government is composed of socialists in a hurry. Let me read on:
I am not, of course, saying that all advertising is undesirable.
Isn't that a frank admission; not all advertising, just the kind of advertising that the bureaucrats think would be good for us. Let me read on:
I am saying that we have a tiger by the tail.
I don't quite follow that, but I presume if I took the time I could understand it.
Or, to vary the analogy, we have got our economy into a state of distorted incentives that makes us feel compelled to run faster and faster in order to stand still.
He has got something there, Mr. Chairman. That is what this Government has been doing, running faster and faster in order to stand still.
The individual business, of course, cannot do anything about this; it cannot contract out of the race while others are in it. The only profitable course is generally to try to do more and better advertising.
Then he goes on to say this:
In principle, there is no reason why advertising should not be taxed, like liquor or gasoline or thousands of other more useful things. But since in effect Government at present subsidizes most advertising to the tune of a half, through its allowance for tax purposes, the better first approach probably is to refuse to allow advertising, and perhaps other merchandising expenditures, for tax purposes.
Socialism at its worst never espoused a philosophy like that. Where would private enterprise be if it had not been for advertising? How would expansion within our country take place if the philosophy of Mr. Kent- apparently now that of the Government- were carried into effect? Then he says:
This would be, of course, a considerable upheaval.
The Minister laughs because he has read all this nonsense. He knows it all by heart and he really does not have to listen. Mr. Kent says:
It might well be approached in stages-
They are not going to abolish advertising all at once.

-in the first year adding back, say 25 per cent of advertising expenditures to a corporation's profits for tax purposes, 50 per cent the next year, and so on. That would give an opportunity for adjustment, not only to the advertisers but also to the newspapers, radio and television. I do not think, incidentally, that the lessening of their dependence on advertising would in the end do anything but good for the media of communication-
I would like to know how the media of communication could exist if they did not have advertising, but apparently I am misinformed in that connection. Then he says:
-Though for their sake-
That is for the sake of the newspapers that are denied advertising.
-it would require some offsetting tariff on the advertising content of foreign publications entering Canada-not as a discrimination, but in order to prevent inequality.
This is where the paternity is established. We are being asked to carry out the policies of the 1960 conference, and apparently this has an appeal for the Minister of Finance and the Government. Mr. Kent says in effect that if we got rid of advertising by these gradual reductions, 25 per cent in the first year and 50 per cent the next year, there would be a considerable upheaval, but he says it will not be a panacea.
This advertising proposal is not, of course, put forward as a panacea. I am not claiming it as something that will fix up our tax problems once and for all.
Then with becoming modesty he says:
I am not pretending to complete certainty that it is the right thing to do, though I am quite sure that it would yield very great benefits, and I will take a lot of persuading that there are comparable disadvantages which at all offset the benefits. However, my only basic purpose is to use it as an illustration of the approach to taxation that we should take-
Then he says this:
If, for example, we did reduce advertising-
I hope the Minister absorbs this because he can learn how he can increase taxes and make us feel good about it.
If, for example, we did reduce advertising, it would thereby become easier also to raise existing taxes on consumption-liquor revenues, gas tax, vehicle licences, real property taxes, and general sales tax. Our provincial premiers could better have their day.
What a philosophy. First he says to the people, you shall not advertise. They will have that much more money available, by being protected against being induced to purchase what, in the bureaucrats' opinion, is not good for them. They will have that
June 15, 1965

much more money available to pay taxes, including the sales tax. Then he says this:
Having mentioned property taxes, which so closely affect the most poverty stricken of our three levels of government, I would say that here increases seem very reasonable. While a general capital gains tax has many undesirable features, and certainly is not to be preferred to increased taxation of inheritance, there is a very great deal to be said for a specific tax on increments in property values, which are the consequence mostly of public decisions.
There is a compendium of economic direction by the man who has been set apart and anointed as the person who has the solution for Canada's problems. In the course of this very interesting monologue he said this:
In effect advertising is an expenditure that aims at higher consumption rather than increased efficiency.
Direct advertising expenditures in the United States last year were over $11 billion. They have doubled in nine years. This leads to waste, the waste of scientific ability in research that produces nothing but entirely trivial modifications of products for the sake of sales gimmicks.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Apparently this is the philosphy of the Government, because Mr. Kent has been raised to the position of director and controller of the war on the poor. Mr. Kent then went on to say this:
If one had to express the greatest inefficiency of our economic system in a sentence, it could well be that too much of our brain power is devoted to selling soap and too little to creative effort in science, in thought, in the public service. If I were Mr. Khrushchev it would be this above all that would give me confidence that my system was going to work.
He adds this:
It is the proper role of Government to step in and alter the incentives: simply to leave advertising less attractive and then leave every business to run its own affairs-
Apparently that is the idea. That principle was advocated last night by the Minister in the course of his remarks when he said "We do not intend to interfere with freedom; this is actually being done for the good of Canadians". Mr. Chairman, all through the ages those who would direct and control are always activated by the highest purposes, filled with a surplus of idealism. And having those qualities they do not want mankind to be deprived of the benefit of their views.
There are many other quotations which I might put on record. I do not intend to do so at the moment. I say, first of all, that these principles which are being applied are not those of the O'Leary Commission; they are based upon something entirely different,
Income Tax Act
the philosophy of social security to which I have just referred.
The freedom of the press in a society of free men depends upon commercial freedom of the press, freedom from direct or indirect Government subsidies or other forms of control. The irony of the present situation is that the Government purports to assist the press by making it impossible for outside competitors to compete. The fact is that these budgetary proposals will bring about a degree of Government control not known in this country, and not known in any country today which has inherited the British tradition of freedom.
I sum up by saying to the Government in the strongest possible terms, withdraw this measure. In 1964 the Government did withdraw, and various Members of the Liberal party sitting opposite today were quoted as being entirely opposed to what was then being considered. I suggest that today those same people should speak out in the strongest possible language against a course of action which, will inevitably lead, to a degree of control over the press which cannot and ought not to be countenanced by Parliament.
Over the years I have spoken on behalf of freedom. When I argued for a Bill of Rights, those sitting opposite said such a bill would have no purpose and no effectiveness. The law books say otherwise. Indeed, only yesterday it was announced in the press that it was expected the United Kingdom would shortly be bringing in a Bill of Rights modelled on the Canadian Bill of Rights.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As one who believes in freedom, as do hon. Members in all parts of this House, I make an appeal to the Government. Throw this legislation overboard. Remove it. Throw this bill out. Withdraw it, now. Every invasion of freedom during the years has been made by people who were filled with enthusiasm for worthy objectives but who had not thought the matter through. Every invasion of freedom, begun as a pathway, has become a highway. It is because of this that I hope the Minister, having already displayed on so many occasions a capacity for withdrawing from what was not proper or appropriate, will act so as to gain the admiration of Canadians generally as well as that of the press which believes in freedom- as he believes in freedom-and as do the people of Canada as a whole.

I should now like to deal with paragraph 10, which in effect says that the cost of landscaping of property by a taxpayer for the purpose of gaining income may be deducted from income for the purposes of determining taxable income. So far he has not given a clear answer to that question. I certainly hope he makes this clear, because in the irrigation districts of Canada-I am speaking now particularly of southern Alberta-the cost of land levelling is a major expense in the operation of farms.
What is more important, Mr. Chairman, is that proper land levelling in these irrigation districts increases the potential production in some cases by more than 100 per cent. That is possible because of the even distribution of water. What is also important is that the cost of spreading water across lands that are properly levelled is substantially less than in respect of undulating surfaces. What is even worse is that there is no capital cost allowance for land; therefore even the actual cost of levelling cannot be included in any category in respect of which depreciation can be claimed. The irony, of course, is that Mr. Diefenbaker is the author of the principle which Mr. Pearson would translate into law. Not at all. This is a problem magazine. In fact most of the Canadian business publications are problem magazines. We also have trade journals. In most trades or callings there are a number of publications, but in the trade magazines no effort need be spent to induce the public to read the ads. Now, the main problem is this. The three specific magazines to which I referred, the consumer magazines, cannot make any profit, which is why they are in trouble.
Because of competition.

Not because of competition, as an hon. Member says; it is because of unfair competition. To get down to the truth of the matter, this unfair competition comes from two magazines at the present time. Time and Reader's Digest. Time magazine is a completely independent United States magazine which stands foursquare against two things, political partisanship and the Democratic party. Reader's Digest has been called the poor man's "Paradise Lost". These two magazines have their printing costs borne in the United States, and their periodicals overflow into the Canadian market and enable them to undersell advertising which would normally go to Canadian magazines and periodicals.
I will not say much about Time and Reader's Digest; as I have said, the right hon. gentleman opposite has indicated that these two should be exempt. This is a fait accompli, in that they are already exempt; but it is not our fault that the right hon. gentleman pinpointed these two magazines for exemption. However, I wish to point out how this legislation will be of assistance to other magazines.
Along this line of thought I should like to refresh the minds of hon. Members in regard to trade publications. Maclean's is published only because its owners publish trade magazines which are profitable, and it is the profits from these trade magazines which keep Maclean's going. Even at the present time a very greedy eye is cast on these profitable Canadian trade magazines by United States concerns. I could name one, but I think most of us know which it is. They would like noth-

I am not saying for one moment that if we help these magazines to continue in business everything will be all right within a number of years. The fact is that the magazines themselves will have to improve and find new formats and new ideas. Canadian magazines will not be able to save their souls through this legislation. But when you consider that in the United States the advertising dollar is moving into the printed page, into the printing media, and that magazines in the United States, through efforts on their own behalf, have been able to pull themselves up by their own shoelaces and are now out of the red into the black, I dare say that the same situation will apply in Canada given time. Mr. Chairman, I know the hon. Member who just asked for a count is anxious to get away, but I will not detain him much longer.
There is another problem facing our periodicals, and it is not a United States or a foreign problem but a Canadian problem. I should like to illustrate some of the difficulties our magazines get into. We note that our weekend magazines are not only surviving but are
June 15, 1965



making a great deal of money through a completely new method of distribution. I am not saying that all magazines will have to adopt it, but given enough time they will be able to do so. But unless this legislation is implemented, more and more United States-owned magazines will adopt the same principle now being used by the two magazines I have mentioned, and will eventually be able to undercut the advertising dollar. In that event our Canadian magazines will be unable to continue.
There is one other matter I should like to raise. At the present time some of the parent companies in the United States advertise Canadian companies and Canadian goods in United States magazines which overflow into Canada. Although this cannot be termed Canadian money directly, indirectly it is because these parent companies in some cases charge their Canadian subsidiaries for a portion of the advertising dollar. I think the terms of this resolution rectify this position, and incentive will be given to permit some of the advertising dollar to stay in Canada.
If I thought for one moment that Canadian periodicals had no chance to survive I would not support this legislation, but I am sure they do have a chance. It is well recorded that the magazine is coming back into its own. I feel confident that Canadian magazines will do everything they can to devise publications which are readable and sell advertising; they just need a little bit of time. This legislation will provide the time. It will allow Canadian magazines to remain in Canadian hands and to survive the period they have been going through. As our population increases we will then be able to have not only three or four Canadian magazines, but quite a few more. The fact is that in proportion our population is increasing more rapidly than that of the United States and the number of Canadian readers is also increasing more rapidly. I honestly and sincerely believe that the Canadian periodical industry will survive, largely due to this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on the income tax resolution in Committee of Ways and Means may I first of all say that the defence put forward with regard to the newspaper control legislation is at best the weakest that could have been offered and represents a very poor defence of the Government's intention to show favouritism toward two wealthy United States magazines which, as was said earlier, are masquerincome Tax Act
ading as Canadian by publishing Canadian editions.
There are a number of things that concern me about the income tax resolution in particular. When the Minister brought down his budget he announced a number of proposed changes that cannot be found in the resolution, and may not be in the bill when it comes before the House. Actually we are all well aware of the fact that the budget gives notice of the Government's intentions and the bills that follow carry out the intentions announced in the budget.
The budget White Paper said that we are now in the fourth year of an expanding economy which started in 1961. I might add that with the devaluation of the Canadian dollar and the huge grain sales to Communist countries the expansion of our economy has continued. However, in the budget the Minister said that he feels the economy needs further stimulation and he has $250 to $275 million to pour back into the economy, or perhaps I should say that he proposes to take that much less from the economy through taxation. He suggested in the budget and in his outline of this resolution that the best way to do this is by an income tax reduction of 10 per cent. As the hon. Member for Edmonton West pointed out, this was perhaps the best political way to make a reduction in taxation, but it was a very poor way from the point of view of stimulating the economy of the country. The Minister could have turned to many other avenues if he really believed that the country needed further stimulation at this time.
Certainly it is a fact that the cost of farm loans has been increased tremendously. I wonder whether the Minister considered making any changes in the Estate Tax Act. This would have permitted more money to be poured back into the economy than will be provided by this paltry 10 per cent reduction in income tax, which does not apply to large incomes. Land prices have tripled in the last five years and to some extent this has been brought about by the easing of credit for the purchase of land. This has caused estate taxes to become out of proportion with the real value of estates now subject to taxation, or that will be in the future. Certainly such a move would have resulted in a greater amount of money being poured back into the economy than is represented by the amount of $250 million to $275 million, because this amount is being spread so thinly that it will provide very little stimulus to the economy of the country.

As was suggested by the Minister in his speech yesterday, he could have reduced the sales tax on production machinery. In reviewing the budget speech one sees that the Minister pointed out there that in the past few years costs of production in Canada have risen to a greater extent than in the United States. In what position does this place Canada? In a very poor competitive position in relation to our greatest competitor. We import more from the United States than any other country and we export more to the United States than to any other country. Therefore we should take careful note of the relationship between the cost of production in Canada and the cost of production in the United States.
The Minister admits that costs of production have increased greatly in Canada and are greater than in the United States. Therefore it is obvious that one of the costs he should have removed in this resolution is the 11 per cent sales tax on production machinery. But no, he did not do so. Such a move would not get him too many votes if an election were called. He felt that a 10 per cent reduction in personal income tax would be the best move for this purpose. He felt that a reduction of $250 million spread across the country would affect more people, and this was his greatest concern. I think he has made a great error in this regard. He may be stimulating the Liberal party by this 10 per cent income tax reduction, but certainly he is not stimulating the Canadian economy. One could add that perhaps that was his intention in any event.
I do not want to deal with some of the provisions in the resolution at this time, but I should like to refer to paragraph 10. As a rule, changes proposed in budgets are for the purpose of directing the economy and, as we always hope, improving it. Sometimes they also plug loopholes. It would appear that paragraph 10 of the resolution is opening up something rather than plugging a loophole. In subparagraph (a) of paragraph 10 the words "to a person with whom the taxpayer is dealing at arms length" are used. As suggested by other speakers, anybody who has any dealings with a lawyer soon learns that the term "arms length" is one that makes for a great deal of debate. What is dealing at arms length, and what is not, is always questionable. Subparagraph (a) is in these words:
(a) to a person with whom the taxpayer is dealing at arms length and who is the lessee of property owned by the taxpayer, to obtain the cancellation of a lease on such property.

In other words, the purpose is to provide an income tax exemption, but the whole clause hinges on the phrase "at arms length" and, as is often said, it certainly opens up a can of worms. Certainly it opens up the avenue to many a loophole.
The second subparagraph is no better. It provides an exemption for an outlay or expense for landscaping property used by the taxpayer for the purpose of gaining or producing income. There is nothing at all to stop a person from doing an expensive landscaping job on a home he is now leasing, claiming the cost as an expense and then moving into the home the following year or two years later.
It seems odd that the Minister went out of his way either in the last budget or the one before to prevent businessmen from claiming what he said were unnecessary business expenses, and yet he is now taking this action. I know he put a ceiling on expensive cars. He said that businessmen do not have to buy expensive cars and that anything over $5,000 would not be allowed as an exemption. Then he went on to say that businessmen's travelling expenses and so on would be looked at very closely by the Income Tax Department. Now, in this budget, he is saying that you cannot buy an expensive car, but you will be allowed to do a tremendous job of landscaping if you wish. Really, all we are doing is plugging loop-holes one year and opening new ones the next.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
Paragraph (c) is so poorly worded that it is not clear. It refers to the clearing of land or the laying of tile drainage for the purpose of carrying on a farming business. This will be considered for exemption. You immediately wonder if this includes the levelling of land. What is the farmer going to clear the land from-bush, rocks, or is it merely rough terrain? The hon. Member for Medicine Hat thought he saw the Minister nod his head in agreement when the hon. Member suggested it might include the levelling of land for irrigation purposes. One would certainly hope so. Why is it not set out in the paragraph? Why is there a reference to the laying of tile drainage? Why would not the construction of a drainage ditch be every bit as good? Certainly this is another method of improving farmland and thereby enabling the farmer to increase his income.
Then, in discussing changes in the Income Tax Act which might benefit the agriculture industry, one recalls that in the budget speech
June 15. 1965

the Minister suggested further income tax changes might be made to benefit that industry. He said, as reported on page 436 of Hansard:
X am also proposing some changes in capital cost allowances to help farmers who are facing difficulty in marketing com and other grain crops in areas where there is a shortage of grain storage facilities.
The Minister goes on to suggest that under this plan provisions will be incorporated in the regulations of the Income Tax Act. I say to you, Mr. Chairman, why are these provisions not spelled out in the bill? I believe that Government by regulation really defeats democracy. No one sees the regulations until they are passed. No one sees the regulations until they are in effect or until he comes up against them. Then people ask why someone did not suggest changes in these regulations. I am firmly convinced that government by regulation opens up an avenue around democracy and I, for one, do not like it.
In the same budget speech the Minister goes on to suggest another avenue which will be opened up around democracy. He states, and I quote:
An important tax concession will also be provided to encourage industry to take new steps to prevent the waste products from their operations polluting our streams and lakes. This will take the form of an amendment to the Income Tax Regulations to permit capital expenditures made until the end of 1966 by businesses primarily for the purpose of preventing water pollution to be deducted at the rate of 50 per cent.
Here again we have changes announced to the Income Tax Act, but little more will be seen of them, as I understand the procedures in the House. They will be implemented in the form of regulations and be completely lost to the House and to the people until they come face to face with them.
Returning to the provision concerning grain storage, we note that new grain storage facilities constructed during the period May 1, 1965 to December 31, 1966, will be covered. In other words, a little over a year and a half will be given for the construction of these grain storage facilities. The Minister goes on in his budget speech to suggest that after the construction of these facilities is completed on December 31, 1966, a period of four years will be given for write-off purposes in so far as income tax is concerned. Last week end the Alberta Wheat Pool opened a new grain elevator in my constituency. Since the building was opened after May 1, 1965, I wonder how the regulations will be applied to that grain elevator?

The Minister suggested, as will be seen from page 436 of Hansard, that grain storage facilities may be built by individual farmers or taxable co-operatives. In other words, the wheat pools could take advantage of this provision. Surely, the Minister should give us some idea-he has not as yet-as to when the regulations will be applied. If a building were constructed after May 1, 1965 but not completely paid for, would the regulation apply to the whole of the cost of the building, or only to that portion which had been paid? Surely we should have some opportunity to debate this provision and perhaps enlighten the Minister and the department concerning the best possible regulations to facilitate the grain industry in both the corn belt of Eastern Canada and the wheat growing areas of the Prairies.
The Minister referred to "grain storage facilities". The question immediately comes to mind, what is going to be classified as "grain storage facilities"? Do we mean an elevator, a feed mill or some temporary building? A building may only store grain for a matter of a month, six months or a year, but the primary purpose of an elevator alongside a mill may not be considered, under these regulations, to be permanent grain storage facilities. I wonder if the Minister or his department have considered the possibility of such conditions arising? Surely, we should be given, before we pass this resolution, some idea of what the changes in the Income Tax Act will be. Surely, we should be given some further light with regard to the proposed provisions in the budget which could prove to be helpful to the farmers of Western Canada, as well as Eastern Canada. This is especially true in the light of the plans that are out for rail line abandonment, which may or may not be proceeded with this year or next year. It may be that companies in Western Canada would be well advised to make a drastic move and rebuild a great part of their grain storage facilities during this period of 16 or 18 months. I do not know.
Surely, one could judge the possibilities better if the Minister gave the details of the proposal in the resolution now before us. Surely if this means government by regulation it defeats, to a large extent, proper representations on given subjects such as this. As I said, in effect this is an avenue around democracy and I do not approve of it. I hope that later in this debate the Minister will deal more explicitly with these matters.

for because gentlemen like Mr. O'Leary and Mr. Johnson favoured a Canadianism which has some parallel, I suggest, with the kind of Canadianism of which the present Minister is at times accused.

The hon. Member is not suggesting he is consistent?

In the main, Mr. Zimmerman of Reader's Digest led the lobby in the periodical field for Reader's Digest and Time. Time has been a little cuter and less interested in a popular approach than Reader's Digest. Time would much prefer direct contact with Cabinet Ministers, particularly with Ministers like the Minister of Industry, who has a relationship through his constituency with the operation of these magazines. To give Mr. Zimmerman credit, I think he is the handsomest and most affable lobbyist I have encountered, with one of the best illustrative and prose presentations I have encountered. On the other hand, the main lobby against Time and Reader's Digest and for Canadianism in the periodical field has been the people who sponsor Weekend Magazine, Mr. Farrell and Mr. Walker of the Montreal Star and the Family Herald Weekly Star.

As a matter of fact, it has such a good market

through so many papers that its success is one of the main reasons, at least in my opinion, why the Toronto Star Weekly has suffered a decline in circulation from one million to less than 700,000 copies.
