The real oddball in the lobby field was the role of Maclean-Hunter publications. I suppose other hon. Members have encountered them. One month you are lobbied, and the next month you telephone Maclean-Hunter and you cannot even get an idea what their policy is. I have come to this conclusion: Maclean-Hunter accepted one of Mr. Zimmerman's arguments that the proper thing to do was to reach some stability in the magazine field-"let us stop fighting with each other and organize a magazine bureau to make advertising in magazines more popular, supplement each other's co-operative efforts and wrest back revenue from television, radio."
Is Saturday Night included in that argument?

Yes, Saturday Night is included in that argument. There is one other factor. It seems to me that since the really profitable business of their operation is in the trade field, Maclean-Hunter began to get very frightened about the prospect of McGraw-Hill, the most powerful and the most able of the United States trade publishers, moving into Toronto. There were rumours they had taken a lease on certain land in the Toronto area and were planning to get into this field.
Magic to find, there is a provision in this legislation which will prevent United States trade publications coming in from now on. It looks to me as though Maclean-Hunter were prepared to keep quiet about Time and Reader's Digest because the trade publication threat from the United States had been blocked. And I think they were suborned to a minor degree by Mr. Zimmerman's arguments that in co-operation lies a golden future. But the reality of the situation at the present time is that Reader's Digest and Time are still with us and, I suggest, they are not Canadian publications.
I recognize the kind of pressure they can apply. I have a paper mill in my constituency which produces the paper for Time and

June 15, 1965
Income Tax Act
Reader's Digest. It was almost like magic how suddenly the management and workers there, including the unions, began to fire in correspondence to me demanding that Time and Reader's Digest be left alone as good Canadian publications consuming good Canadian paper-particularly that manufactured in the constituency of Port Arthur.
Surely the hon. Member is not suggesting that the union was seduced, too?

I am suggesting that where dollars and cents are concerned it is easy to lose sight of one's national ideals. I am firmly convinced the loss in terms of the paper market would, in time, be filled by Canadian publications if Time and Reader's Digest were put in their proper places.
You had better worry about your own seduction.

There are more ladies on the other side of the House than we have over here.
The point which needs to be made as we look ahead to the future is that by this legislation Time and Reader's Digest are set up for the foreseeable future in such a fashion that their main editorial content can continue to be drawn, in the main, from outside the country. I think anyone with any sense would agree, on looking at these United States publications, that this content is not produced in Canada in the main. I feel very strongly that this legislation should specifically wipe out parts of 12A(2). Later on we will attempt to move an amendment which will do this, although my colleagues and I are finding it difficult to draft. We intend to move an amendment which will specifically point to Time and Reader's Digest and classify them as non-Canadian publications under the intent of this resolution. At the very least, when this amendment is moved we should receive from the Minister a thorough explanation of his conversion from a Canadian nationalist, the author of Troubled Canada, the projector of the Canada Development Corporation, the architect of the Canada Student Loans Plan and the author of Let's Buy Back Canada, to a man who believes that Reader's Digest and Time magazine are really Canadian publications. I think we are at least entitled to that explanation.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
I should now like to touch upon the newspaper aspect of this resolution. I have been very interested in this because I happen to

know quite well the publisher of the Toronto Telegram, John Bassett, and a few other publishers with whom I have had some contact. One of the things that intrigues me is the argument advanced by a few publishers that this provision that no presently Canadian-owned newspaper shall be sold to or allowed to get into the hands of a foreign corporation is a threat to the freedom of the press. I cannot for the life of me see that there is any threat in this regard to the freedom of the press.
I do understand why Lord Thomson is raising a bit of a fuss, because his feelings have been hurt as a result of what happened to him in relation to Canadian citizenship. After receiving the "lordship", which he sought for so long, because of the regulations of our Government he had, in a sense, to dissociate himself from Canadian citizenship.
I find Lord Thomson the most attractive newspaper publisher I have ever encountered. Whenever I have gone to see him he has taken out his books and shown me how much money he is making in his various operations, and he has done so with such delight that I can understand why universities such as the University of New Brunswick and the Newfoundland Memorial University fight for the right to have him as a chancellor or donor.
This is a man who has gone from a start up in Timmins-I always felt he should be Lord Porcupine of Timmins-to those great places of the world, to the point where he often merits a full page of coverage as the greatest press lord of all in such august periodicals as the New York Times and New York Tribune.
Do not be jealous.

The hon. Member suggests that I should not be jealous. Let me assure him and other Members in this House that I genuinely find Lord Thomson to be one of the most interesting and pleasant persons I have ever encountered because he is so excited and pleased at being so successful. I think it is wonderful that a man can go from being a defeated Conservative candidate in the east end of Toronto to a lord in the House of Lords in England consorting with the great and mighty, visiting Russia on even terms with the heads of state.
Lord Thomson has a world-wide operation, and naturally he has the kind of holding company argument and the typical attitude of the businessman of large scope who does not want national boundaries to get in his way. Lord
June 15. 1965

Thomson looks upon newspaper publishing primarily as a business. You will remember what he said in England. He wanted to set up a Labour newspaper, if that was possible, not because he was Labour in his attitude but because he thought there was a market for that kind of newspaper, and it did not bother him to be the owner of a Labour or Socialistic newspaper, because the main thing was to have the ownership and advertising revenue.
This kind of publisher is a rarity, I grant you, not particularly caring what axe he is going to grind in his newspaper as a whole; but this attitude also reveals how little nationalism, particularly from a Canadian point of view, we are likely to get from Lord Thomson; and that is a worth-while revelation. It seems to me that his objections are a perfect example of the international operator, rather than a Canadian citizen.
I sometimes feel that when Mr. Bassett complains, it is because his conscience is bothering him in connection with his television operation. I do not know whether he was forced to, but he certainly did go to United States organizations to borrow capital in order to keep the television operation going. My point in respect of the publishers' objection is that if foreign ownership, as a principle, which many of us including the Minister of Finance and Members of this party advocate, is wrong because it strikes at the future of our nation and our national ethos, then this also applies to banks and to almost any field, primarily and essentially to the field of communications, through which an influence can be brought to bear on the culture, attitude and philosophy of the people.
Anyone who argues that this resolution, in so far as it applies to newspapers, should not be introduced, has to accept the fact that if it does not now, it is only a question of time until the kind of rationalization of capital that exists in Northern America and in the western world will lead to the accumulation of a Canadian chain of newspapers by an outside organization. Some of you are entitled to ask: Would that be bad? If I could get the publisher of the New York Times to come up here I think he might be a preferable owner to Lord Thomson, in terms of the kind of newspaper we would have. However, the whole point is, in essence, what are we going to get in terms of ownership; and that would not be Canadian ownership.
If it is vital to have a C.B.C., then it is vital to have Canadian publications owned by
Income Tax Act
Canadians, wherever possible, and I support the proposition very strongly that this legislation, which will restrict the sale of Canadian newspapers in future to foreigners, is an excellent bit of legislation. I cannot see how it is going to affect the freedom of the press. It will affect the freedom of publishers, and the freedom of the publisher to dispose of his goods by selling to a foreigner.
One must recognize that this could cost the present Canadian publisher a lot of money. It is quite conceivable that the greatest capital resources of Chicago or New York, or organizations from those areas would be able to come and offer more for the Toronto Globe and Mail or the Montreal Star than any Canadian group; but even in that regard there is no way that one can look at this situation and envisage how, even if the largest of Canadian newspaper operations came up for sale-I suppose the largest of all operations is the Southam operation- it would be beyond the resources of a group of Canadians; and I am sure there would be purchasers.
The final point I want to make in connection with this whole matter is in the form of an appeal to the Government and to the Minister, on this question of Time and Reader's Digest, that we have a free vote. Perhaps it is too much to ask of or too tough on Government supporters to have them stand up and go against this whole question of Time and Reader's Digest, without something more than a tacit understanding that they are encouraged to do so by the Minister and the Government. I know that to take this approach would be a most unusual course for the Minister to follow.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I know it is unusual to advocate it, but it does seem to me that through lobbying over recent months we have had a very thorough discussion of this matter, and the issue of Time and Reader's Digest should be settled on the basis of Canadian nationalism and the way it is looked at in the future. I would suggest that the fairest way to get a vote, one which we will be prepared to accept, is to have a free vote, so that we can see on which side of the question Members of the House line up, and whether Time and Reader's Digest are to be naturalized, corporate Canadian citizens from now and forever more.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak briefly regarding this particular item in the resolution. Many of us in this party have felt very strongly for some time about

June 15, 1965
Income Tax Act
this legislation. I think it would he reasonable to say that the Minister deserves the congratulations of many of us in this House, including many hon. gentlemen opposite who have expressed some feelings in this regard in the past, despite the speech made by their leader today. He deserves our congratulations because we have been talking about legislation of this general nature and with this general theme for five or six years at least. It has been actively discussed, yet nothing has been done.
I might point out that nothing was done by the previous Government. Now something is going to be done, and for that reason I think this is a gigantic step in the direction of preserving the Canadian identity in this media, certainly of our newspapers and to a great extent our periodicals, and as such it should win the commendation of a great many Members in this House.
I should like to refer to some of the arguments made by the Leader of the Opposition today. He seemed to centre his attack upon the legislation on the basis that it was a limitation of the freedom of the press; that it was an inroad into that sacred right which we in this country have always maintained, namely that the press should be free and independent. I too was completely mystified by this approach of the Leader of the Opposition when one considers that it was the O'Leary Commission, a Commission constituted by his own Government, which made findings which were certainly very close to the precise recommendation which has been made by the Minister today and to establish this fact I intend to quote a few paragraphs from the report of the O'Leary Commission.
I am also surprised at what must be considered tantamount to a rather hypocritical stance on this question, when one considers that the right hon. gentleman himself proposed legislation of an almost identical nature in the field of periodicals, providing for similar exemptions of Time and Reader's Digest. If it can be argued that legislation of this nature is a limitation of the freedom of the press, then it is a limitation on the freedom of the press irrespective of whether Canadian periodicals or Canadian newspapers are involved. The right hon. gentleman when he was leader of the Government, and those who supported him who are present today, espoused the principle which is inherent in this legislation both in respect to periodicals and magazines. I think it is very difficult for any of them to evade that charge.
[Mr. Munro.l
Getting back to the attack made on this legislation on the basis that it limits freedom of press, in this regard I think I should refer to the report of the O'Leary Commission which deals at considerable length with this question. At page 7 of the report, the first paragraph, the following appears under the heading of "The Need for Self-Sufficiency":
That guarantee, we are convinced is vital.
That is, the need for self-sufficiency.
For while Canada and the United States may have the same basic cultures, they each at the same time have domestic and other tasks and problems-political, social and economic-which differ widely. Canada's particular responsibilities, her government, her constitutional structure, her ideals and aspirations, her memories and milestones, even her discords, are facts in her existence which cannot be approached understanding^ or usefully by communications media owned or controlled in another country, even though that country be friendly.
I emphasize that the O'Leary Commission refers to "communications media"-generalizing here-owned or controlled in another country, even though that country be friendly. The report goes on to refer to media, and surely no one would argue that newspapers are not part of the communications media. The report states:
Only a truly Canadian printing press, one with the "feel" of Canada and directly responsible to Canada, can give us the critical analysis, the informed discourse and dialogue which are indispensable in a sovereign society.
In view of this it is difficult for me to understand how the Leader of the Opposition and hon. gentlemen opposite can state that the O'Leary Commission did not recommend Canadian ownership of our daily newspapers. I do not know how anything could be more unequivocal in this regard than the paragraph to which I have just referred contained in the report of the Commission itself.
Again we see what I think is an unfortunate and tragic contradiction in policy between the former Conservative government and the speech of the Leader of the Opposition today. Here we have two basic contradictions. The right hon. gentleman attacks the legislation because of the exemption of Time and Reader's Digest, yet he provided these exemptions in his own legislation. He also attacks the principle of the legislation because it is a limitation on freedom; yet he evolved that very principle when he himself brought in legislation with respect to periodicals. He now denies the main, central theme of the report of the O'Leary Commission, a Commission set up, as I say, by his Government and which reported to his Gov-
June 15, 1965	COMMONS
emment. So that the Leader of the Opposition is clearly wrong when he states that the O'Leary Commission did not recommend Canadian ownership of our daily newspapers.
Another, more disturbing facet of the speech of the right hon. gentleman is that it seems to be contrary to the impression he himself created throughout the country. In 1957 and 1958 he was supposed to be a leader who was going to preserve our Canadian identity. He was the one who espoused the cause of Canadian nationalism. He was the one who accused the former Liberal Government of that day of being too pro-American and not sufficiently concerned with the protection of Canadian rights. Yet in this speech he goes against the very grain of that position with which he has always endeavoured to identify himself; Canadian identity. In his speech he has denied the necessity for the protection of our Canadian newspapers as far as Canadian ownership is concerned.
Six o'clock.

speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-9, to incorporate Principal Life Insurance Company of Canada.

He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of Bill S-9 is to incorporate Principal Life Insurance Company of Canada.
The bill originated in the Senate, where it was passed on May 27, after the Banking and Commerce Committee of the Senate had heard witnesses and studied the measure.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that this proposal to incorporate Principal Life Insurance Company of Canada implements a petition from a group of men from the business and financial community of the City of Edmonton, known as the Collective Group.

The petitioners, Mr. Speaker, as indicated in clause 1 of the bill, are a group of Edmonton businessmen well experienced in the field of finance, retirement and savings plans and insurance. Their experience in this field extends back to 1954. The fact that they are coming to the Parliament of Canada for the incorporation of this insurance company, which will form part of the group known as the collective group, is additional evidence of the very buoyant and burgeoning economy of western Canada. I must say that this is the case not only in the Province of Alberta but also in British Columbia, and there are indications that it applies to other parts of Canada.
If we look at the financial history and economic development of our neighbours to the south, we will see that the corresponding region of their country did not really go forward until they had a nucleus or network of their own financial institutions. I think the progress in Canada is a clear indication of the necessity not only for financial institutions based in Central Canada but also for those operating in western Canada on a branch plan basis. In this regard I might indicate that in the last session of the Provincial Legislature of Alberta seven life and trust companies were incorporated for operation in that province. However, the matter in hand, the incorporation of Principal Life Insurance Company of Canada, comes to the other place and to this House because this company intends, although it wishes to

June 15. 1965
Private Bills
operate primarily in its first years in Western Canada, to operate throughout the country and even on an international plane.
From the examination of insurance legislation in the past we know that the Government of Canada is tightening up its requirements with regard to capitalization and surplus. The Federal requirement is $500,000 of capital and $500,000 of surplus. In Alberta the requirement is somewhat less but it will be brought up to $750,000 in total by the end of the year. Under Bill S-9 this company is to be incorporated with a capitalization of $1 million, and may I say that no appeal to the public will be made for the sale of its stock.
I invite approval of the bill on second reading and then examination in detail before the Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs of those witnesses that the committee may wish to examine. The capital requirement for this company is not going to be sought from the public. Already the collective group has set aside $1 million from its reserves for the capitalization of this company.
To deal with the history of the collective group briefly, Mr. Speaker, may I say that during the early years of the operations of the company the collective group expects to concentrate its efforts on the development of Principal Life Insurance Company of Canada in the western provinces. Eventually it is hoped that the company will do business throughout the whole of the country. It already has within its own network 36 offices in Canada and two in the United States, the collective group having had certain companies organized and approved under the appropriate law in the United States. It also has the necessary personnel.
Let us look at some features of this group. First of all, what is the management team? This group, in operation for about 11 years, has shown itself to be quite a successful one. Its assets have increased more than 2,400 per cent since 1956 and in fact they amount to some $56 million according to its 1964 balance sheet. In eight years the number of holders of the group's investment contracts has risen from 4,700 to more than 63,000. The group has its own selling, administrative and investment divisions. So far as the selling of insurance is concerned, this is done through its direct sales force operating out of its various regional offices. May I say that this group was the first to introduce a massive computer into western Canada. It was the first to bring

in an I.B.M. system 360 computer. It has a staff of 400.
I do not want to appear to be boasting, but this particular group has also been operating under the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act for over 11 years. Therefore they have full knowledge of the insurance and trust business and of portfolio administration. Of its 75 head office employees, 31 are university graduates and all of the senior personnel in the accounting department are chartered accountants.
May I say that I heartily endorse the organization of this company. The petitioners are listed in clause 1 of the bill. They are Donald M. Cormie, a practising barrister and head of this financial group, Ralph Perrin Forster, a man of long experience in financial areas, V. R. Stewart, a member of the management group, John W. Kennedy, a solicitor, Kenneth Marlin, a business executive, and Lynn A. Patrick, a solicitor and active counsel for the Principal Life Insurance Company.
[DOT] (6:10 pjn.)
It is instructive to note what this group has done in so far as the generation of savings is concerned as compared with other life insurance companies. The savings generated in the Province of Alberta by the collective group in 1964 amounted to $7,379,000. Now, the Sun Life was next with some $5,958,000; Prudential, $3,296,000; Manufacturers Life $3,077,000; Great West Life $2,487,000; Confederation Life had something like $1,336,000. Some Members may say that this represents a lot of money going into life insurance within the Province. However, it is a matter of statistical record that notwithstanding the fact we have a lot of insurance companies in Canada, and more are being incorporated, only 25 per cent of the population of Canada is covered by life insurance. There is, therefore, a great market in Canada for life insurance, for the accumulation of savings and for the placement or investment of those savings funds in the development of Western Canada.
I am sure hon. Members from Western Canada will share my view that moneys made available are then invested by Western Canadian businessmen who are aware of conditions there. I would say the same thing of the Maritime Provinces, British Columbia and the Central Provinces. I do not believe it is necessary to say that Boards of Directors concentrated in Toronto and Montreal necessarily have the best appreciation of the investment opportunities in other parts of the country. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I invite all

Mr. Speaker, I rise to give wholehearted support to the request of the hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) that this bill be referred to the committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. I should like also to give full support to his statement that the economies of Alberta and British Columbia are buoyant and that it is the natural outgrowth of these expanding and buoyant economies that financial institutions of this kind come into existence. It is a fact also that financial institutions of this kind and other types assist in further expanding the economies of these areas.
I find it rather strange, however, that it is only on rare occasions we can get the hon. Member for Edmonton West and other Progressive Conservative Members to pay this kind of tribute to the Provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. Usually they have some very severe criticisms of these two Provinces. Sometimes I suspect this is mostly because there are Social Credit Governments in both of them. Nevertheless the fact is that the economies of these two Provinces have expanded faster during the past few years than those of any other part of Canada. It is natural that financial institutions should desire and attempt to set up there. We know it may be only a coincidence, but we think there has been some deliberate action and that it is because of these Social Credit Governments out there that the tremendous expansion has taken place.
We hope that there is not going to be some kind of Federal action that will inhibit this expansion. I have received a telegram today from the City of Medicine Hat which had prospects for some new industries establishing there. However, as a result of the designated or so-called development areas announced by the Federal Government, some of these industries are taking a second look at it, especially in view of the inducements and incentives offered by the Federal Government in this other legislation. I know that this might not be the right place to advance this kind of argument. However, I do feel strongly that we do not wish to have discriminatory legislation that will result in having misplaced industries. Surely it is not the purpose of the Federal Government to penalize those areas that have been expanding, and actually hold them back by legislation that makes it difficult for an industry to establish in these fast growing parts of Canada.
I do not want to say more about it, except that we welcome the opportunity to support this kind of financial institution. We hope there will be a change in the attitude of the Government so that we can have the Bank of British Columbia established in Western Canada for the purpose of assisting the expansion of the economy out there as well. We hope that there will be some change of attitude so that this expansion can be helped rather than hindered at this particular time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
The few remarks which I have to make tonight are my own and stated as a private Member. I want to say a few words about our banking system. I want to advocate the incorporation of more banks in Canada. More specifically, I want to advocate the incorporation of banks such as the Laurentide Bank and the Bank of Western Canada which we are discussing today. For these reasons, I am opposed to the amendment presented to the House which would affect the incorporation of the Bank of Western Canada by giving the bill a six months hoist. I am opposed to that. I believe that we should deal with this matter. I am referring to the incorporation of the Bank of Western Canada by sending the bill to the appropriate committee of this House in order that it may be considered on its merits. I hope this will happen, too, in respect of the Laurentide Bank.
Now, in approaching this matter of banking, I should like to explain my own position clearly. I should like to say, quite forthrightly, and I think this is agreed to by many other Members in this House, that I am a Canadian first and I am a British Columbian second. I am sure all hon. Members would put the nation before their Province in all cases. This is one of the main reasons I am opposed to the incorporation of banks which are owned by Provinces. It is for this reason

June 15, 1965
Private Bills
I draw a distinction between privately owned banks such as the Laurentide Bank and the Bank of Western Canada and the proposed Bank of British Columbia which, in this instance at least, would be partially controlled by the Government of British Columbia.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
I believe as a second principle we should have less government rather than more government. Whenever we have a choice we should have one level of government involved in the regulation of an activity, rather than several levels of government. For this reason I believe that as money and banking are specifically reserved, under the B.N.A. Act, to the Government of Canada, no attempt should be made to bring the provinces into the business of banking.
The B.N.A. Act is quite clear on this matter. Section 91 reads as follows:
-the exclusive Legislative Authority of the Parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the Classes of Subjects next hereinafter enumerated; that is to say-
15.	Banking, Incorporation of Banks, and the Issue of Paper Money.
16.	Savings Banks.
It goes on further to say:
Any Matter coming within any of the Classes of Subjects enumerated in this Section shall not be deemed to come within the Class of Matters of a local or private Nature comprised in the Enumeration of the Classes of the Subjects by this Act assigned exclusively to the Legislatures of the Provinces.
In other words, banking, the incorporation of banks, the issuance of paper money and savings banks are matters under the jurisdiction of the nation.
I am sure no Canadian would really want to see different coloured dollar bills in our provinces. In other words, to have a nation we must have one monetary system, and to have an effective monetary system we should have one central bank and chartered banks run by private enterprise which are clearly subject to the laws of Canada. To me that is an effective banking system.
Several hon. Members have referred to the prosperity of Western Canada. B.C. is very prosperous, and so is Alberta, but I do not attribute this entirely to the provincial governments. I attribute it partly to the genius of the people who live there and to the great resources of that part of Canada. In fact, I think the natural advantages of Western Canada far outweigh the natural advantages of the rest of Canada and this is one reason why now, and on into the future, Western Canada will be more prosperous than the

rest of the nation. I do not attribute this to any government, and certainly not to any individual political party.
I wish to refer briefly to what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) had to say in respect to the incorporation of banks. He underlined the fact that the B.N.A. Act clearly assigns to this Parliament exclusive jurisdiction over banking and the incorporation of banks, and he went on to say:
Even a limited ownership of shares of a bank by another government, whether it be a foreign government or a provincial government, could place such a government in a special position of power or influence in relation to that bank.
Such a situation might lead to differences of opinion between this government and another government, and to confusion over who exercises authority in regard to the bank.
This is crucial, and this authority must be clearly identified. It must be clearly identified as the national authority.
The principal argument used by the province of British Columbia is that provinces have control over property and civil rights; that shares in any enterprise are property, and hence a province can have control over bank shares, and can properly buy a controlling interest in a bank.
I suggest that provincial governments do not have all the powers of a private individual. Also their concern is with property and civil rights within a province, and not extending beyond the province. Certainly banking, in the manner that the bank of B.C. would be incorporated, does extend beyond one province, in this case from B.C. to other provinces, and beyond our Canadian provinces to other countries in the world. In other words, it extends into an area which is clearly one of federal jurisdiction.
I believe we need more banks. Certainly the Porter Royal Commission indicates this. We need more competition in respect to the lending of money. This will drive interest rates down and make money readily available. In the 1880's we had 30 to 40 banks. Today we have eight. We have five which are entirely national, two confined to Quebec but operating under federal law, and one which has branches in Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver.
We need more banks in the West. We also need bank headquarters in the West because of our economic prospects and because of the growing financial power of Western Canada. The government of B.C. made a very interesting submission to the other place. It indicated that today the economy of B.C. alone is greater than that of the Atlantic region. Our
June 15, 1965

population is comparable. The turnover in respect of money is substantially greater. Some of the figures are illuminating. For example, labour income in B.C. is 55 per cent greater than that of all the Atlantic provinces combined. Cheques cashed are nearly two and a half times as great as in the Atlantic region.
If one thinks not merely of B.C. but also of the Prairies having an economy half again as large as that of B.C., he knows we are dealing not only with a growing region but a very important one in economic terms. In population terms it challenges Quebec, and in economic terms it is comparable to Ontario. It is the most rapidly growing and most vital part of Canada, and needs not only more branch offices but bank headquarters as well.
The government of B.C. is fond of indicating that the Bank of America, the biggest bank in the world, has its headquarters in California. It does not, however, say that the Bank of America is owned or was initiated by the State of California. It is a private bank operating under the laws of the United States and is part of the U.S. federal reserve system. It is totally responsible to the laws of our neighbouring nation to the south. It is not akin to a provincial bank. It is not a state bank; it is a privately owned bank.
Numerous other reasons are given by the government of B.C. as to why there should be a Bank of B.C. Our friends in the Credi-tiste party are blocking the incorporation of other private banks in order to bring the Bank of B.C. forward but, if they will allow me, I will destroy the remaining arguments advanced for a provincial Bank of B.C. One argument is that it would assist in making Vancouver a centre of Canadian finance. If the Laurentide Bank were incorporated it would help us to attain that objective.
Another argument they advance is that a chartered bank must succeed. Since when have chartered banks in Canada not succeeded? We have not had a significant bank failure, nothing like the failures in the United States, even in the depression years of the 1930's.
A third argument is that the bank should be concerned primarily with B.C. I suggest that all banking institutions are concerned about making money, are concerned about investing in going concerns in whatever part of Canada they do business. Therefore that qualification would certainly be met by banks like the Laurentide Bank and the Bank of Western Canada.
Private Bills
They also argue that bank shares should have a relatively stable market value. Most of our Canadian bank shares, because of the solvency of our banks under a very fine banking system, have that stability.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
They also suggest that the provincial government can be of practical assistance to a bank. I suggest that the Government of British Columbia will be putting its surplus funds, tax revenues and income from other sources into the Bank of British Columbia exclusively.
Finally, the problem of professional management would be met. Canada's chartered and other banks have been very well managed and I suggest the Bank of British Columbia would be recruiting most of its management from the staff of the chartered banks. Therefore this argument of a lack of professional management falls to the ground.
I should like to refer briefly to the nature of the directorate of the proposed Bank of British Columbia. The gentleman proposed as president is Mr. Einar Gunderson, senior partner of the accounting firm of Gunderson, Stokes, Walton & Company. He is among other things chief fund-raiser for the Social Credit Party in the Province of British Columbia. He is also the executive vice president and a director of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway, a British Columbia socialistic enterprise. He is executive director of the British Columbia Hydro and Power Authority, another Government-owned agency. And he is a member of the British Columbia Ferry Authority. He is one of the principal confidants, if not the closest personal friend, of the Premier of British Columbia. The claim that this would not be a politically influenced bank falls to the ground because of the personalities involved, certainly that of Mr. Gunderson. This is the man who recently stated that, for more than a decade he had been raising money for the Social Credit party's election campaigns purposes. He has been raising it in the name of the British Columbia Free Enterprise Education Fund. Mr. Gunderson is, of course, an officer of a number of socialistic enterprises and some of these have been socialized within a relatively short period of time. He personally played a major role in bringing them under Government ownership.
Now I should like to consider the scale and scope of the proposed bank. This Bank of British Columbia would have a capitalization of $100 million, that is to say, of the same order of magnitude as the Toronto-Dominion Bank. In order to be profitable it will have to attract

all of the savings of all individuals, all firms and all institutions in the province, besides those of all the Crown corporations-and then some. Were it to confine its activities exclusively to British Columbia there would be no room left for any private bank whatever. It would have the effect of driving free enterprise out of all banking in British Columbia, driven out by the man who is proposed as President of this Bank, the person who has been soliciting contributions in the name of the British Columbia Free Enterprise Education Fund. In my view, those who have been contributing to this fund have actually been contributing to the downfall of private enterprise in several important areas, one of the most significant of them being commercial banking in Canada.
What would happen if Quebec were to decide to follow this example, as is entirely likely? Eventually we might have as many as ten provinces taking an equity interest in chartered banks whose policies they would influence or control. Private enterprise would be wiped off the map in Canada in this field. The Bank of Canada would remain the agent of the Federal Government but it would have to deal with ten separate provincial banks. We could not look forward to a continuance of informal discussions held once a month or more frequently between the central bank and the various chartered banks. Instead we would be committed to a series of Federal-Provincial Conferences bearing on monetary policy. Imagine what might happen if inflation began to get under way and the Federal Government decided to pursue a tight money policy. The Province of British Columbia might resist such a policy as being against the interests of many of the people in that province. So there would be a dillying and dallying between two different levels of Government. Federal-Provincial conferences perform a useful function but I doubt whether they could be effective in managing the monetary policy of this country. I can imagine the Premier of British Columbia saying, for instance: I will go along a little distance with this tight money policy if you will turn over your offshore mineral rights to the province; instead of bringing this issue before the courts we shall have it out around the table during this so-called conference on monetary policy.
What view would other countries take of this monetary Balkanization of Canada? England has one of the most successful banking systems in the world. It has a national bank and a number of private banks subject to the

law of the United Kingdom. A Labour Government was in power in the United Kingdom for a number of years but it did not see fit to permit the Balkanization of its banking system. I suggest to Members of the New Democratic Party that their endorsement of the Bank of British Columbia renders their ideas for planning on a national basis nonsensical.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
This is important. The New Democratic Party wants to plan our way of life more effectively. It says the Government should move into more areas of economic activity. I can think of no activity more essential to economic planning than the formulation of monetary policy, and I cannot imagine that a national Government headed by the hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) would look with favour on ten provincial premiers coming to the bargaining table, each with a particular banking policy, each with ideas as to whether there should be tight money or easy money, ideas as to how credit should be advanced, and so on.
As one who endorses the free enterprise system I firmly believe we need a monetary policy with only one set of rules and only one level of Government involved. This Parliament should establish the ground rules upon which banks should operate right across the country-a system flexible enough to meet all our needs as they arise. This would give mobility to industry and develop the economy to an increasing extent for the benefit of all Canadians. National unity alone requires that the setting up of provincial banks should not be entertained by this Parliament and that this proposal to establish a Bank of British Columbia should, in particular, be rebuffed. On the other hand, private banks, including the Bank of Western Canada, should be incorporated in order to make our present system more flexible and more effective.

speechtext: A longer answer to the question is that there are certain latitudes permitted to chartered banks, observing the law in its strictest form, and within those latitudes, if all chartered banks owned by provinces were to throw their weight one way, it would make it very difficult to put any particular policy into effect.

I have a supplementary question. Is that true of the present shareholders of banks? Are they able to frustrate federal policy by exercising the power they have as a result of the shares they own at the present time?

speechtext: I suggest that there is a great variety of interests among the shareholders of our different banks and that this variey of interests reflects the national interest to a considerable extent, and that to the extent it does not reflect national interest it allows the will of the majority to prevail.

Mr. Speaker, I have been very interested in listening to the speech of the hon. Member for Coast-Capi-lano. I am sure he has assisted the Social Crediters and the Creditistes in their marathon talk-out of any proposed bank charter.
The hon. Member's speech dealt with a great many things other than the application for charter of the Bank of Western Canada, in respect of which some of us are particularly interested. The hon. Member complained that the control of the British Columbia Bank might lie in the hands of a few, and that its power might be directed in certain ways at the whim of a political party or of a few individuals.
The hon. Member never once tried to defend the application for charter of the Western Canada Bank.
Yes he did.

Someone suggested that he did. I read the remarks made by the mover of this bill, and she at no time, in moving first or second reading, refuted some of the charges made before the Banking and Commerce Committee of the Senate of 1964. I intend to refer to those hearings in greater detail later on.
If the hon. Member for Coast-Capilano has no objection to the granting of a charter for the Bank of Western Canada I do not understand why he objects so strenuously at this time. Let us be very clear at this time that a very few powerful people will have control
of the proposed bank, and that those people are not people resident in Western Canada. That being the case, what is the difference in respect of the application for the charter of the Bank of British Columbia?
When the Premier of the Province of British Columbia appeared before the Senate Committee, and I have the report of that committee in my hands, although I will not have time to read the relative portions, he stated he would be agreeable to reducing his interest to 5 per cent or 10 per cent. In view of that fact what is the difference in the attitude taken by the Government in respect of these applications for charters?
As a result of a rigid cross-examination by a member of the other place the information was revealed that 49 per cent of the stock of the proposed Bank of Western Canada, at least under the terms that existed in respect of the application last year, would be held by three people. We have now heard an ardent spokesman for the Government say that it would be a terrible crime to give a charter to a bank, only a fraction of the shares of which would be held by the Premier of the Provincial Government, who wishes to develop these vast resources of his Province and who takes it upon himself as a responsibility to develop those resources for the benefit of the people of that Province. On the other hand, we hear the same spokesman and other Members of his party avidly supporting an application for a charter of a bank which supposedly wishes to develop Western Canada but which in fact will benefit very few more than three individuals. After listening to the speech of the hon. Member I am afraid that the hon. Member has more than convinced me, and perhaps this is the first time, that the sponsors of the Bank of British Columbia should expect, as a right, to receive a charter.
The hon. Member for Coast-Capilano has not convinced me that the charter requested by the bill now before us should be granted, and I shall point out in the time available to me why I am not convinced. Perhaps at some stage the mover and those people who ardently speak in favour of this bill will present some sound arguments for this application for a charter, rather than spend their time condemning another application.
The mover of the bill pointed out, as recorded at page 1260 of Hansard, that the capitalization of the new bank is to be increased and that 4,720 certificate holders are from western Provinces, whereas 830 are

Of the proposed 6,099 shareholders only 233 are from outside of Western Canada; but what control would those 233 shareholders have? That is the point of interest to us. It is my feeling that they would have the greater control, and this is supported by the evidence of Mr. Stevens as reported at page 59 of the same proceedings of that committee, which met on May 6, 1964.
At page 60 of the proceedings, in reply to a question, Mr. Stevens stated that the group of companies involved are The Wellington Finance Corporation, Limited, Canadian Finance & Investments Ltd., and York Trust and Savings Corporation. After rigorous examination it was discovered that the York Trust Company would hold 33,000 shares, that the Canadian Finance Company would hold $2,250,000, or 150,000 shares of the proposed capitalization, and that the Wellington Finance Corporation would hold $3,750,000 or 433,000 shares of the capitalization. In other words 43 per cent of the capital of that proposed bank would be held by those three companies, and that is only part of the picture.
Under the proposed Bank Act no individual, person or party shall own more than 10 per cent of the shares of any proposed chartered bank. I believe that the holding of a bank charter is a right of Canadians generally and that this Government or Parliament should not interfere with that right. I believe that the base of any bank charter should be spread as broadly as possible, rather than being narrowly confined as would be the case in respect of this application for a charter for the Bank of Western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, nothing has led me to believe that there is any great change in this

application from that which was presented earlier. I do not suggest there are not any changes, because obviously there have been some, but let me attempt to show that it does not matter where the shares are, but that what is important is where the capital and voting rights lie. Forty three per cent of the capital of the new bank is to be held by three companies, as indicated by the evidence given before the Banking and Commerce Committee of the other place on May 6, 1964, as recorded at page 60 of the proceedings of that committee.

It appears that 43 per cent of the capital of the new bank would be held by these three companies; and one of them holds practically a controlling interest in all three.

I would like to emphasize the indirect nature of that, though. For example, X would have a 49 per cent interest in one company-
There are three other shareholders, but it is not fair to suggest that a 49 per cent interest does not in fact control a company. Certainly we are not naive enough to believe that anyone with a 49 per cent holding in a company does not, in effect, control it.

To save any misunderstanding there-I am trying to be correct in my statement-I will say that the next largest holder would be William J. Mollard. He appears in the prospectus. I am trying to be correct as to whether myself plus Bell plus Mollard control-those three certainly control.

principal shareholders of the controlling interest in the new bank applying for a charter. He also pointed out under examination that these three people could quite conceivably sell their shares to other persons or to another person, so that you could have a controlling interest in this proposed Western Canada Bank in the hands of one company.
I must say I have been looking for something to set my fears at rest. I looked for something from the mover when she moved second reading of the bill and from the ardent spokesman who favoured so vehemently the Western Canada Bank, rather than the bank sponsored by the Province of British Columbia. But I heard and saw little to set my fears at rest. However, I notice that the capitalization of the proposed bank is now larger than it was last session. I may be of a suspicious nature, Mr. Speaker, but three men went before the other place in the last session of Parliament and asked for a charter. There are only eight charters in Canada. These three individuals want the ninth. Therefore, why should we in this Parliament not suspect that they would come back in this session masquerading under the name of the Western Canada Bank? There was quite a few years ago a Western Canada Bank. As the hon. Member for Coast-Capi-lano (Mr. Davis) said in his speech, he did not believe for one moment that chartered banks ever lose money, and I would agree with him on that. But for some reason or other they do sell and they do amalgamate. I do not think for one moment, when the old Bank of Western Canada, so named, eventually amalgamated with the Standard Bank and the Standard Bank amalgamated with the Bank of Commerce, that in any one of those transactions the parties or persons concerned lost a nickel. Therefore I think it is the duty of Members of Parliament and those in the other place very carefully to examine the application for this charter, and whether or not the charter will be placed into the controlling hands of a few. They should investigate whether or not these people intend to carry out the declared operations of this proposed bank.

Mr. Chairman, prior to private Members' hour I was referring to the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition in which he indicated that this proposal involved some limitation of the freedom of the press. I was quoting from the O'Leary Commission report, a Commission which I would reiterate was set up during the administration of the right hon. gentleman, reporting to the Government of that day. As reported at the bottom of page 7 the Commission has this to say about the freedom of expression argument:
In our society, freedom of expression-and therefore of the organs of expression-is so firmly established as to require overwhelming justification of anything that might be construed as interference by the State. So sacred indeed is the freedom of expression-or freedom of the press, which is but a function of all freedoms-so essential is it to our way of life that its protection benefits from every doubt of State measures which concern it.
This Commission was not established to devise means of curtailing the freedom of expression, nor to fashion means to in any way limit press freedom. It has not conceived it to be its function to restrict opinion in any way. But this is not to say that venerable and sanctified cliches about "press freedom", shouted at the Commission through so many of its hearings, should deter it from a sincere accomplishment of its instructions and much less from an honest discharge of its duties to arrive at conclusions and make recommendations, whether or not they entail legislation. There is need to remember that freedom of the press is not an end in itself, but only a function of general intellectual freedom; to remember that no right includes a privilege to injure the society granting it; to understand that a great constitutional doctrine cannot be reduced to a mere business convenience, and that the press is but a Fourth Estate- not a whole community.
Leaving out a few lines, the report continues:
At the same time, however, it has viewed with distaste the sight of fundamental principles of democracy being sent to act as decoys in the interest of commerce.
I think that this amply demonstrates the point made by the Minister of Finance in his introductory remarks last evening when he stated that this proposal was in no way a limitation of the press, that it in no way was directed at any curtailment of the dissemination of information, but rather all that it did in effect was to limit the sale of newspapers by their owners to interested Canadian purchasers rather than to foreign or non-resident purchasers. In other words, it is a limitation

in the business area but it has nothing whatsoever to do with the dissemination of information or editorial policy or the position taken by newspapers so far as the free expression of ideas is concerned. As was also indicated by the hon. Member for Port Arthur, I cannot for the life of me see any validity in the argument that the proposal limits or is an invasion in the area of freedom of the press.
I should like to deal a little further with the O'Leary Commission report. An interesting thing is that the O'Leary Commission not only recommends the imposition of limitations on the periodical press in order to preserve their Canadian identity but even goes further and suggests that in the future we may have to think in terms of other legisla-ion of this type, though still not dealing in the area of dissemination of information, still not dealing in the area of editorial policy or the encouragement of conflict of opinion but, if you like, dealing in the business area, in the area of physical ownership. On page 8 of the report there is the heading "The National Interest", and this is the justification given by the Commission for the type of limitations which are proposed in this legislation. The justification is the national interest. In this regard the Commission said:
There is, after all, practically nothing a government can do without impinging upon the rights and privileges of some so that they may harmonize with those of others with which they may conflict. The constant redefinition of rights and privileges is the continuing task of government. That this process is difficult, there is no doubt. However, even in a matter as sacred as the freedom of expression limitations have been applied in the past: no publication has the right to libel.
There is one inherent limitation.
It is not inconceivable that new limitations may be necessary in the future, seeing that with the increased importance and mounting power of mass communications, there must be a corresponding gain in the power and importance of the relatively few people who control the media, and, therefore, a decrease in certain rights of other individuals in the community.
I take that as an indication by the O'Leary Commission of their concern over the degree of concentration of ownership in the whole mass media field. I take it as an indication of concern that has been expressed not only by the O'Leary Commission but by many others, because the degree of concentration of ownership in the mass media field, not only newspapers, has grown to an alarming extent in Canada. I suggest that in this particular paragraph the Commission foresees that maybe a somewhat similar type of development will have to occur in Canada, as took
June 15, 1965

place in England with the establishment of the Shawcross Commission, to go into the whole area of mass ownership in the media field because, as the O'Leary Commission has stated, "there must be a corresponding gain in the power and importance of the relatively few people who control the media and, therefore, a decrease in certain rights of other individuals in the community".
It has always been recognized as a fundamental function of any government in a free society that it must protect the rights of the individual, and if this concentration of ownership should occur to the degree that it diminishes the rights of the individual we can perhaps foresee legislation in this field also. So the principle of national interest is there. Our country and other countries in our democratic society have recognized that there is a fundamental duty to protect the individual against concentrations of power and to protect the national interest against foreign influences.
This is the justification for this legislation. This is the justification advanced by the Commission which formed the basis of the legislation as it was first introduced by the former Government. Therefore, for the former Prime Minister to indicate in the House today an attitude in direct conflict with and diametrically opposed to a bill his own government had on the order paper based on the recommendations of his own Commission is, to me, simply incomprehensible.
I think this also points out another interesting development in the political evolution of the ideas of the Leader of the Opposition. Professor George Grant has recently written a book entitled Lament for A Nation. There has been some discussion of this book in Canada. In it he has identified the Leader of the Opposition as a great nationalist, as one who was opposed to the power complex and pressure groups in Canada, as one who advocated that the Canadian identity must be preserved. It must be disillusioning indeed to his champion, Professor George Grant, who extolled the Leader of the Opposition to such heights, that now the Leader of the Opposition should today criticize and indicate his lack of support for this type of legislation. I think it would be interesting to refer to one portion of the book. As found on pages 16 and 17, Professor Grant states:

There is something naive about Diefenbaker's attacks on Toronto and Montreal business in the 1963 election, particularly in the light of the economic policies his government had pursued from
Income Tax Act
1958 to 1962. It is not surprising that the only literate and established voice on the side of Diefen-baker in the election of 1963 was Senator Grattan O'Leary, who was himself caught in the trap of romantic nationalism. Senator O'Leary also was a supporter of both nationalism and capitalism. He could presumably combine the two because he thought the leaders of Canadian capitalism after 1940 were still nationalists. There seems less excuse for such nonsense from the publisher of a great eastern newspaper than from a western lawyer. It is, nevertheless, startling that the western lawyer could still believe capitalists were nationalists after a term as Prime Minister. In short, Diefenbaker did not understand the economic implications of Canadian nationalism; he could not appraise the class structure realistically, and therefore he could not formulate the economic policies that were necessary if nationalism was to be more than rhetoric and romance. Even after his defeat, he does not seem to have learnt these lessons. As Leader of the Opposition, he attacked the measures, put forward by Walter Gordon to limit the control of this country by American capital.
Here we have it from this author, a great defender of Mr. Diefenbaker and his administration indicating his disillusionment with the inconsistencies and contradictions in the positions and postures taken by the Leader of the Opposition with regard to the policies advocated by the Minister of Finance last year and within the first year of our taking office. Again, we have an illustration of the Leader of the Opposition opposing such policies here today. It becomes somewhat of a tragedy that Canadians have learned to look to the Leader of the Opposition as the personification of the champion of preservation of the Canadian identity, and yet today we have opposition to legislation that I would suggest goes to the very heart of any real effort to preserve any type of Canadian identity at all.
Surely, Mr. Chairman, we must concede that in the ownership of newspapers we have a very essential element of the whole mass media field. When we concede that we have the whole field of the mass media involved, then we are talking about one of the fundamental areas of ownership in our whole way of life. If we should allow the mass media to fall under the control of non-residents or foreigners, we would have no semblance of independence or sovereignty left. This would surely erode the very foundations of any aspiration toward any type of Canadian independence or Canadian sovereignty. As I say, it is just beyond my powers of understanding when we are talking about the mass media here, when we are talking about legislation designed to preserve Canadian ownership in the mass media field, when we acknowledge that the mass media is one of the essential

Income Tax Act
elements In forming a national identity, and when we are proposing the legislation which is so necessary to preserve that identity, that the Leader of the Opposition seems to have given up any hope of plans for the preservation of the independence and sovereignty of this country.
I noticed another thing in the position taken by the Leader of the Opposition, which was disturbing. I refer to the fact that no alternative policies were advanced. I find it impossible to believe that the Leader of the Opposition or any other Member of this House could complacently sit back and watch one of our newspapers like the Globe and Mail, the Toronto Star or the Montreal Star fall into the hands of non-residents. I do not believe that any Member of this House could accept that type of development with peace of mind. It would be bound to cause considerable pain. It would be bound to cause considerable aggravation to every Canadian because he would realize this was a further example of the encroachment of foreign ownership and control of our country. This would be an area in which the dissemination of ideas would be involved, and not just physical assets.
If the Leader of the Opposition is just opposed to the method of implementing this proposal and is not opposed to the over-all aim of the legislation, one would have thought that the party opposite would have advanced some alternative proposal by means of which the purpose of this legislation could be accomplished. No such proposal was advanced. In fact, this has been the position of all of the critics of the present policy. They admit that the Federal Government has no other legal means by which its aim could be accomplished. They realize that under the British North America Act we do not have the power to legislate with regard to the ownership of property. Perhaps this is the reason no alternative proposal was brought forward.
Surely a party that has gone on record from 1958 to 1962 as being most concerned with this problem could find an alternative, otherwise it is sheer irresponsibility to oppose this proposal. They must certainly accept the challenge of coming up with some other adequate means of accomplishing the same end, or support the Government on this particular piece of legislation before us tonight. If they do not do so, then they are guilty of the greatest contradiction, the greatest reversal of policy I have ever heard in this House during the short time I have been here.
I should like to refer to one or two other matters. One suggestion I have heard ad-

vanced in some quarters as an alternative means has been some type of subsidy arrangement advanced by the Federal Government to these periodicals. I am referring now to periodicals rather than newspapers. This would be a means of preserving the Canadian periodical and preventing it from disappearing as a result of this unfair competition to which so much reference has been made today. Anyone who advocates that type of arrangement certainly would be flying in the face of those who indicate concern about the limitation on the freedom of the press, interference with the press by Government.
I have yet to hear anyone indicate that in a subsidy arrangement there is not an intangible influence by the Government upon the periodical involved. Perhaps this is the reason we do not hear the subsidy argument advanced in this House. I think we must look back and accept the fact this legislation is inevitable. We must look back to our own Royal Commission and the conclusions to which it has come. We must look back to what almost happened to the Globe and Mail, when a non-resident investor submitted a bid and undoubtedly if his bid had been higher the Globe and Mail, which holds itself out as being Canada's only national newspaper, would have fallen into the hands of nonresidents. Developments such as these undoubtedly prevailed upon the minds of the Government and the Minister of Finance when introducing this legislation. Developments such as this injected a degree of urgency.
[DOT] (7:20 p.m.)
In conclusion I would like to reiterate the point that this legislation is consistent with the type of legislation we have in other areas respecting mass media and the communications field. It is consistent with the limitations involved in the radio field to preserve Canadian ownership. It is consistent with the limitations involved in the television field to preserve Canadian ownership. None of us heard any criticism from any opposition party when those controls were imposed and in fact the origin of such limitations goes back many years. No one heard any such criticism about limitation of freedom when only periodicals were involved. We just began to hear it when newspapers were included.
This legislation is in the national interest. It is not a limitation on expression. It is not a limitation on freedom of the press. It is consistent with other legislation dealing with the mass media field. If we desire any sem-

blance of preserving Canadian identity in the important field of mass media it is in the national interest that this Chamber should approve this measure.

Mr. Chairman, we have just listened to the second part of the band concert accompanying the introduction of this resolution. Last night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) told a rather sad story in glowing terms when he dealt with the question of income tax. Tonight the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, another member of the band, tried to convince us that this measure was worth its weight in gold.
This resolution gives me, once again, the opportunity to emphasize the viewpoint of the low wage Canadian. As a matter of fact, if I have decided to say a few words on this resolution, it is because the Canadian wage-earner is taxed more than ever before in the history of Canada. On the other hand, besides being taxed as he has never been before, he has to cope with the cost of living which has never been as high since Confederation.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I will try once again at this time to make representations on behalf of the small wage earner.
Nowadays, heads of families in the low income bracket are up against all kinds of difficulties; they cannot make both ends meet and every year their situation gets worse. Even if the Minister of Finance, as I said a few moments ago, announced in glowing terms a 10 per cent reduction, we find, after closer examination, that many people will not benefit by this reduction. One cannot help but think that this government has only one objective in mind: to assist people in the higher income brackets as much as possible and those in the lower income brackets as little as possible. This is not the first time, Mr. Income Tax Act
Chairman, I have risen in this house in an attempt to convince the Minister of making changes with regard to personal exemptions. The Minister would have accomplished his duty and done something for the small wage earner had he announced an increase in personal exemptions and deductions for dependants.
I should like to say once more to the Minister that, in these days, it would only be fair and reasonable for single persons to have personal exemptions of at least $1,500, while the exemption for married people should be increased to $3,000 from $2,000. In regard to dependants eligible for family allowances the exemption should be $350 at least, instead of $300. As for dependants over 16 years of age who are not in receipt of family allowances, the head of the family should be able to claim an exemption of $600 instead of $550.
A few moments ago, when I listened to the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), I was under the impression that he intended to convince us that absolutely nothing had been done to help employees in the lower brackets before this government took office.
For his information, I will point out that when we assumed power in 1957, or at least at the beginning of 1958, we raised the personal income tax exemptions for dependants so that all large families could benefit further from deductions. I believe we thus set an example which could be followed by this government. During electoral campaigns, the Liberals are lavish with their promises; once in power, they should live up to those promises. I know that I would be out of order if I proposed the removal of the 11 per cent tax which has largely contributed to increase the living costs. I shall therefore abstain from pursuing the subject.
There is another field where the minister could do something to help those who really need help. This involves increasing immediately the old age pension from $75 to $100 monthly for all Canadian citizens age 65 or over.
When the minister dealt with this question some time ago, he announced that pensioners would receive $75 at age 65, but they will have to wait at least four years more. Mr. Chairman, you know that when one reaches the age of 65, one has much less years to live than one has lived. Therefore, chances are that even though the minister's promise may be attractive for our older citizens, the latter will not, in the final analysis, be able to

Income Tax Act
take advantage of the generosity shown by the minister when he announced this change in old age pensions.
Now that the Minister is in his seat, I should like to ask him once again to take my suggestions into consideration, so that something be done for those who are truly in need. I should like first of all to make a brief reference to the general subject which was dealt with a short time ago by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and earlier by my hon. friend from Port Arthur. I will make no attempt to join the Parliamentary Secretary in psychoanalyzing, as it were, the position taken by the Leader of the Opposition but I should like to say something in connection with the questions raised by the hon. Member for Port Arthur-I noticed that the Parliamentary Secretary carefully skirted around them in the course of his remarks about the freedom of the press. I am referring to the proposal which will allow certain editions of Time magazine and Reader's Digest to continue as wholly Canadian publications.
My hon. friend made the suggestion-and I think it is a reasonable one-that this is a question which should be submitted to a free vote by Members of the House of Commons. Despite the fact that this has been brought forward as a budgetary proposal because of the mechanics involved, I do not believe this is really a budgetary matter. I think the Minister of Finance would agree that this is not primarily designed to affect the balance of ways and means; it is a matter which concerns our outlook as Canadians on our culture and its development, and the provision which should be made for the dissemination of such things. While I have made no particular effort to discuss this matter with private Members on the other side of the House I strongly suspect a great many of them are not happy about the present proposal. Indeed, I would be very surprised if the Minister of Finance himself were very happy with this situation. The remarks made by the hon. Member for Port Arthur this

afternoon remind me of a situation in which I found myself a number of years ago when a proposal dealing with this subject was brought forward by a former Minister of Finance, Mr. Walter Harris. As one of the Members of this House representing the then four parties in the Chamber I was invited to take part in a panel discussion in a posh Laurentian resort before a convention of advertising executives. I found myself in the unusual position of being the only person there prepared to support the position taken by the Minister of Finance of that day. The representative of the Liberal party in our group came from a Montreal constituency, I believe. When he rose to speak he announced that this was one of the occasions when he would be bound to disagree with the Government he normally supported. If an arrangement could be made to have a free vote I suspect that a good many of the Government's present supporters might indicate they were not happy with this perpetuation of what is, to me, an unhappy situation. We are not dealing with the true facts of the situation when we regard magazines which are, basically, produced in another country as being Canadian.
I do not believe anyone here would suggest there should be any limitation on the flow of publications into Canada from other countries. I think all of us are in favour of a free exchange of ideas in the international field. But we have a responsibility in this Parliament to deal with a situation where certain publications are able to bring out publications masquerading as Canadian though in reality they are not.

Reference was made in the budget proposals of the Minister of Finance to the matter of providing the opportunity for considering as an expense, if I understand it rightly, expenditures that are made to eliminate or prevent water pollution. This proposal has not been spelled out in any great detail and I suppose this may have been because the Minister regards it as one of the incidental features of his budget. However, as far as I am concerned, I consider this to be one of the more significant suggestions the Minister has made.
I do not know whether or not this will be an effective way of encouraging the reduction of the pollution of our rivers, lakes and other waters, but if this proposal is to be brought forward, which will allow expenditures for the reduction of water pollution as deductible expense, I should like to sug-
June 15, 1965

gest to the Minister that when he brings this proposal forward in its final form consideration be given also to including similar expenditures as taxable expenses in the field of the reduction of air pollution. I feel these two subjects are closely linked. Protection in respect of the purity of our air is equally as important as protection in respect of the purity of our water. I should like to put forward the plea that these things be placed in the same category.
Perhaps I can attempt briefly to indicate why, among other reasons, I have a particular interest in bringing this matter forward. To illustrate my point I should like to quote from some remarks attributed to Dr. Donald Anderson of the University of British Columbia Medical Faculty, who was reported last January as having said that in the Alberni Valley area, where I live, five times as many people suffer from respiratory diseases than anywhere else in British Columbia. This comes about partly because of the particular climatic condition which prevails and partly because we have a very large industry based upon our forestry products.
This matter of air pollution has been of continuing and increasing concern to some 25,000 people who live in this valley, as it has been of increasing concern to people who live in many other parts of this continent, including such places as Vancouver and of course, across the line in the City of Los Angeles, in respect of which we hear a great deal about their notorious smog.
This matter is one about which there is still some uncertainty, and one which requires in my view a good deal of further research. I am glad to say that in a very modest way the Department of National Health and Welfare has made a grant to assist a research team operating within British Columbia to make a comparative study of this particular situation where there is this high level of respiratory disease, and to attempt to determine just how far and in what way these diseases are a result of the industrial effluence which pours out into the air.
Pressure continues to be made on industry to make greater expenditures to eliminate the pollution which even though it may not be as injurious to health as many medical authorities fear, nevertheless, remains a very unpleasant situation with which one must live. In this connection I should like to quote briefly from some remarks made by the Secretary of the Interior of the United States on this subject which appeared in an article published in Pulp and Paper of March 15, 22620-157
