1965. The Secretary of the Interior was referring to the continuous flood of complaints he receives about the subject of air pollution.
Mr. Udall is reported as having said:
The stock argument that these conditions are part of the "price which must be paid for progress" will not be tolerated much longer. Their mounting impatience is caused by justifiable belief that too little is being done to achieve the possible.
Following that argument advanced by Secretary Udall, I believe what he has said certainly applies in this country. Dr. G. H. Bonham, who is the medical director of an area health unit in the Vancouver Island region, from which I come, has been making some study of these matters and has made some public comment in this regard. He refers to the lack of proper bylaws to control pollution, but he states, and I am referring to a newspaper report which appeared in the Victoria Daily Times of November 16, 1963:
-that industries could not be entirely blamed for not using odour and smoke control measures when "the public complacently accepts the smell of money."
He added that good control equipment was not prohibitively expensive

In another report of the same speech by Dr. Bonham, which was carried in the Nanaimo daily Free Press, he is reported as having said:
We are not in complete ignorance as to how to achieve this control. Ask the Swedes!
They employ chemists from the B.C. Research Council (a tax-supported body) to advise them on both the installation and operation of smoke and odour control equipment.
Lack of knowledge is thus not the only limiting factor.
I have sat in at meetings where management of industry has complained about the high cost of increasing the level of pollution elimination, and it on those grounds that under the circumstances, if the Minister is going to move into the field of encouraging expenditure in respect of water pollution, I ask as well that he include also encouragement toward the increasing of elimination of pollution of Canadian air.

Income Tax Act
subject which has become a hardy perennial, as far as I am concerned. In fact, I believe I have raised this question in respect of every budget since I have been a Member of this House. I raised this matter during the discussion on the last budget. The Minister of Finance may recall that support came from quite a number of Members in the House for an amendment to the Income Tax Act which would meet this problem which is faced by workers who, because of the nature of their employment, have to work and live for part of the time away from their normal place of domicile.
I must say, Mr. Chairman, as I listened to the remarks of my colleague from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands regarding the cavalier way in which the Minister apparently went about the preparation of this budget and said "Well, I guess we can afford a little tax reduction so we will make it 10 per cent across the board, and that is that", that I could not help but agree with him that the Minister could have much more carefully considered the nature of any tax reductions that he was going to make. When he introduced his first budget I know he was criticized rather severely in some quarters of the House for having had too much help in its preparation. In this case I think he has gone to the other extreme and has had no help in the preparation of this budget. He has simply said that he will throw out the sop of tax reductions and this is the simplest way of doing it, because it will save any headaches which might be involved in studying how to approach the matter.
I listened to the Minister last night, and if I heard him correctly at that time he made some remark to the effect that he felt that if there was going to be an income tax cut it should be done in a manner which would apply equally to all Canadians in all parts of Canada. I could very well take those remarks as a text for my argument in respect to section 5 (a) of the Income Tax Act. I have attempted to be helpful to the Minister several times in proposing amendments, and if he does need any further help at this time I could refer him to Bill No. C-42, which is on the order paper in the name of my colleague the hon. Member for Skeena. As a matter of fact I think I should say that the hon. Member for Skeena and I are, in effect, co-authors of this particular bill, and if I 
would not be in breach of the Criminal Code I might admit that we had tossed a coin to see whether this bill would go on the order paper in his name or mine. This bill sets forth what, in our view, would be a suitable amendment to the Income Tax Act, the kind of amendment which, as I mentioned to the Minister last year, I felt I was on the verge of persuading the former Minister of Finance, Walter Harris, to introduce in the session prior to the time when he ceased to be a Member of this House.
Without arguing this point any further, Mr. Chairman, I should like to place on the record of this discussion the exact proposal that I should like to see adopted, and I hope that the Minister, in the light of the very sound advice offered to him by the hon. Member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, will reconsider the ill-considered proposal he has made for passing on something by way of an income tax reduction. I should like to see section 5 of the Income Tax Act amended by adding after subsection (2) the following subsection:
(3) Notwithstanding subsection (1), in computing the income of a taxpayer for a taxation year from an office or employment, there shall not be included
(a)	expenses necessarily incurred by him for board and lodging by reason of his employment at a distance from the place where he maintains a self-contained domestic establishment:
(b)	expenses incurred by him for transportation between his ordinary place of residence and his place of employment where, by reason of distance, he is required to live away from home to perform the duties of his employment; or
(c)	expenses incurred by him for depreciation and replacement of tools and special equipment or clothing which are necessarily required by him in the performance of the duties of his employment.
If I may say so, Mr. Chairman, a proposal of this kind, which the Minister is well aware has been suggested by, among others, the Canadian Labour Congress in a number of its briefs to the Federal Government, would be a much better measure in the interests of the working people of Canada than the proposal which the Minister has inserted into his budget income tax resolution, I would guess as a sort of afterthought which will allow the deduction of trade union and professional society dues over and above the minimum $100 deduction. This, I suppose, is a gesture. It really does not amount to very much, but the proposal to amend section 5 of the Income Tax Act for which I have been arguing for so many years would be much more in accordance with the principle of equitable application of an income tax levy on the working people of Canada.

The minister added:
It is true that the interest on the public debt represents an expenditure for the government.

On the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that the Minister of Finance seems annoyed, because we are challenging one of his speeches.

Member to co-operate with the Chair and to confine the remarks he is making so they can be included within the limits of the resolution before the Committee.

Mr. Chairman, I submit to your ruling, but I still think the Minister of Finance is wary of discussion and that he only ventures into a discussion when he is sure nobody can answer him back. It shows a lack of courage of one's own convictions.

Mr. Chairman, I shall abide by your ruling. I know that the Minister of Finance is much relieved because he is afraid of discussion.
Under section 1 of the resolution under consideration and which I quoted earlier, the income tax is reduced by an amount equal to the lesser of 10 per cent of basic tax or $600.
For the low wage earners-but we know that the Minister of Finance is not interested in them

this will mean practically no reduction at all, because it only adds up-and the Minister of Finance gave us the figures himself-to a few dollars for those earning less than $4,000 or $4,500. This 10 per cent reduction will represent a fairly large amount only for those who are in receipt of higher salaries, that is, those who the Minister of Finance has to protect in the house at the expense of the common people, the low income groups. The Minister of Finance agrees to advocate their theory since

he defends them so well and reduces their tax by 10 per cent, a cut which does not apply to the small wage earners.
In my opinion, paragraph 1 of this resolution should be changed and an income tax exemption should be granted mainly to those with inadequate salaries. For instance, we have been suggesting for a long time-and this would not cause the inflation about which the Minister of Finance talks through his hat-to raise the basic tax exemptions to $1,500 for single people and $3,000 for married people. That would at least enable small wage earners to keep the little they have instead of giving it back to the Minister of Finance to allow him to repay the interest on the public debt.
I agree with the Minister of Finance that the interest on the public debt does not impoverish the little man-that is what he said in his speech yesterday. But it remains that out of the income tax collected on the salaries of small and big earners alike, $1.1 billion is used to pay the interest on the national debt.
The Minister of Finance is ready to fight for such a system. As for us, Mr. Chairman, we submit that tax exemptions should be raised to $3,000 for married people and $1,500 for single people.
Mr. Chairman, those are the only remarks I wanted to make at this stage of the resolution.
I would have liked-as I said earlier-to talk a little about the heretical views of the Minister of Finance on the monetary system. Although he knows nothing about the present monetary system, he prefers not to hear the truth and to hold discussions during which he is the only one to speak so that his remarks go unchallenged. Therefore, I leave him to his ignorance.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take advantage of the opportunity presented by this resolution to bring to the attention of the Minister an omission which I feel he will be glad to correct at the earliest possible moment. In the Minister's budget speech and under the heading of "Accelerated Capital Cost Allowance" he makes reference, as found on page 436 of Hansard, very properly, I think, to the fact that he wishes to make some special allowance for facilities for the storage of grain. He takes note of the fact that storage facilities are needed for corn production in parts of Ontario, refers to changes in har-
June 15, 1965

vesting techniques and goes on to say that transportation and grain handling facilities should go hand in hand.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
Now, the matter I want to bring to the attention of the Minister relates to the question of storage facilities for root crops. This is of particular importance to the constituency which I have the honour to represent since part of western New Brunswick, particularly the counties of Victoria and Carleton, are large potato growing areas. In this day when chemical fertilizers are used substantially, the crop per acre is very large. This brings to mind the fact that the planting of the crop and then the harvesting of it is a major operation. The marketing of the crop cannot be carried out unless there are adequate storage facilities. Obviously in the autumn of the year a full year's production has to be harvested and these potatoes must be taken care of for the full year in order that they may be marketed in an orderly fashion. They have to be protected from the frost during the winter and from excessive heat in the spring and early summer, so there will always be a supply of potatoes available for the market.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I hope hon. Members take due notice of your admonition.
The point I was trying to bring to the attention of the Minister was the need for including in these income tax regulations the same sort of consideration for refrigerated storages for the potato crop of New Brunswick as is envisaged for the grain growing parts of Ontario and Western Canada. I believe this question of orderly marketing is most important. The matter of the potato crop itself is very important to that part of New Brunswick which I represent. It is necessary, if people are to be able to conduct orderly marketing, to have access to markets not only in Canada but also in the United States and South American countries. This question of refrigerated storage then becomes most important.
It is with these facts in mind, Mr. Chairman, that I make these brief remarks. I request the Minister to take notice of these facts when he finally brings his bill before

the House. I hope he will make provision for accelerated depreciation facilities for the storage of the potato crop and root crops in general, and I hope this problem will be recognized and dealt with in a satisfactory way.

Mr. Chairman, in keeping with the new rules of the House and the desire for Members to be brief, I certainly do not intend to talk at any great length this evening. My participation in the debate at the moment is motivated primarily by the subject to which the hon. Member for Port Arthur referred, namely, the proposed legislation on periodicals. I was intrigued by the number of speakers participating in this debate who have expressed the opinion that probably the Minister of Finance was unhappy at having to sponsor the proposed legislation on periodicals. I feel this is a tribute to the Minister because I think it is realized, and this probably prompted these observations, that the Minister of Finance has shown a degree of Canadianism that most of us feel is important at this crucial time in the history of Canada.
I believe it is no secret to most Members of this House that the Minister of Finance certainly comes from a background with which I am not too familiar. I believe that by my standards, and the standards of my community, the Minister is amongst those privileged Canadians who are not necessarily waiting for the next pay cheque. Because he is a typical example of big business in so far as success is concerned, I think his concern about the Canadian identity is much more refreshing. Certainly some of the legislation proposed by the Minister was hardly the type of legislation that would necessarily endear him to the closely knit financial community with which he was so closely associated before he became a Member of the House of Commons. I agree with those who sense that the Minister is not too happy with the proposed legislation.
I cannot help but remember my participation in the debate just a year ago. At that time the hon. Member for Edmonton West reminded me that probably I would eat some of the words I uttered at that time. I shall refer in a minute or two to those words. I believe one of the tragedies of Canada, as we approach our centennial, has been our inability to act and believe as Canadians. I believe that we owe much to the Province of Quebec and French speaking Canadians. They cannot take the lazy way out as we English

June 15, 1965
Income Tax Act
speaking Canadians do, when we rely heavily on the periodicals, publications and television programs from our friends to the south. French speaking Canada has had to foster, support and cultivate its own mediums of culture. When we English speaking Canadians cease to fear French Canadian domination in their own province, we will all benefit from the fact that in Quebec we have some distinction from the culture of the rest of America.
There are four fields of communication, Mr. Chairman, radio, television, newspapers and periodicals which have a very definite bearing on the cultural future of Canada and perhaps of Canada as a nation. A year ago, I did express an opinion in the House which I am glad to repeat, and which can be found at page 2122 of Hansard. I said at the time that I felt very strongly that Reader's Digest and Time magazine were American publications, have always been American publications and fully intend to remain American publications. I went on to say that it was my strong view that so far as the editorial content of a magazine was concerned, the nationality of the people who wrote the editorial should be the criterion of whether or not the magazine was Canadian or American.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
In the year that has elapsed I have not changed my opinion. Reader's Digest and Time magazine are American periodicals. I have not changed my desire to help promote those magazines we consider to be Canadian. Where I have differed over the year is whether or not the legislation proposed a year ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) would do anything for our Canadian magazines. Like all hon. Members I have been subjected to the lobbyists of Reader's Digest, Mr. Zimmerman and Mr. Gundy of Time magazine; but nobody, including the hon. Member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) has yet convinced me that any advertising revenue released by the expulsion of Time and Reader's Digest would flow into what we call Canadian magazines.
This is the essence of my doubt a year later. If somebody could get up tonight and convince me that the elimination of Time and Reader's Digest from the Canadian scene would automatically ensure the future of Maclean's, and other Canadian magazines, I would be the first to vote for this legislation; but somehow I am afraid the problems of Canadian periodicals run a little deeper than

legislation to force advertising revenue into the pockets of those magazines.
A lot of us are dissatisfied with this whole thing, but I agree with that section pertaining to newspapers. By no stretch of the imagination can the proposed legislation be interpreted as an impediment to freedom of speech or communication. We must have a free and unfettered Canadian press to write our editorials, to criticize the Government, to bring justice to the fore, to discuss the question of Viet Nam and many other contentious problems where there is dissidence and differences of opinion. There is a danger in having our newspaper editorials dictated to us from friendly sources outside our nation.
If Canada in the next century is to emerge as a nation we must in many ways depend on the strength of our communications in the mass media field. If I am dissatisfied with the proposed legislation it is because it does nothing, absolutely nothing, to divert advertising dollars from those radio and television stations that permeate the perimeter of Canada just below our border in Buffalo, Plattsburg, and similar places. What is good for the goose is good for the gander, and if we are going to attack this thing in the proper manner then it is time we take a closer look at television and radio.
It is a welcome sign that the Minister's proposed legislation will at least eliminate certain abuses. After so many years of bickering Reader's Digest and Time are entitled to be told once and for all where they stand. While I am not particularly concerned for either Reader's Digest or Time as a corporation I am concerned for the employees who work for them, who worry about the future, who would like to know what the future is, if anything, who would like to know whether they are wasting their time away or whether they are living on borrowed time.
By our Canadian standards of fair play we owe some explanation or decision to these people, these employees and other people affected by the industry, so that they may know where they stand. If we intend to run Reader's Digest and Time out of the country, then let us do so, but let us not leave them in a state of abeyance so that their employees and people affected indirectly suffer unpleasantly about their economic future.
In conclusion I would like to reiterate my admiration for the Minister of Finance for being willing to sponsor not only this type of legislation, imperfect as I think it is, but for his willingness to push the Canada Development Corporation, and his willingness
June 15, 1965

to try to establish a Canadian identity in our business. It is refreshing, as I mentioned earlier; and each time the Minister of Finance takes a step in this direction he arouses the animosity of those who were, not his playmates but certainly his business associates for many years. I think the Minister of Finance meets the criteria of a good Canadian, but I think the time has come for us to stop living in the mistaken belief that the simple expediency of punishing Reader's Digest and Time will automatically alleviate the problems of Canadian publications.

When the Minister made his introductory remarks he said the Government was awaiting the report of the Committee on Taxation before making any substantial changes in the tax structure. For years Members of this party have advocated a thorough revision of the whole tax structure, which at present has got to the stage that it is almost impossible to analyse it and find out just what is involved. As time goes on, rather than being simplified it becomes more complex and confusing. When the tax committee makes its report I hope it will make definite recommendations which the Minister will be prepared to implement in order to relieve the tax burden on the Canadian people.
At page 10 of the Report of the Royal Commission on Banking and Commerce we find these words:
We also believe that Canadians want the basic freedom to arrange their financial transactions with a minimum of interference, and have approached our task in this light.
This is a very significant statement because, with the passage of time, Canadians are finding it much more difficult to arrange their own financial transactions. The Government is moving in in every conceivable way, until it seems the taxpayer is hemmed in on every side. The handling of his financial transactions is taken out of his own hands by the Government, under the implied idea that the Government can handle a person's financial transactions better than he can himself.
When this commission reports I hope it will make substantial recommendations with a view to alleviating the burden on the Canadian people as a whole.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
I would like to refer briefly to the 10 per cent tax cut which has been played up as something significant to the economy. It may be an indication that the Government is
Income Tax Act
reversing its position and is moving toward a reduction of taxes. If it is establishing a trend, I think it is worth while, but if this is not the case I do not think it is significant in the over-all picture, bearing in mind that no tax relief is being given to those in the low income brackets. I believe there are other ways in which the Minister could have cut taxes-ways which would have been of greater benefit to the Canadian people. For instance, I believe many Members of this House thought a higher basic exemption would have contributed more than this 10 per cent reduction.
Some time ago the newspapers published an insinuation that we in the Social Credit Party had voted against the raising of the basic exemption for income tax purposes. I wish to state clearly and definitely tonight that the Social Credit Members in this House did nothing of the kind. There was a want of confidence motion brought before this Chamber criticizing the Government for not increasing the basic exemption. It is true we voted against that motion. There was nothing positive about it. Had it carried we would still not have had higher basic exemptions. We therefore took the position that it was not worthy of support. But we have consistently supported the principle that there should be higher basic exemptions. When the figure of $1,000 was established many years ago in respect of a single person it was based on the assumption that in order to secure the necessities of life a basic exemption of $1,000 was required. If this were true so many years ago, how much more true is it that a much higher sum is required today when we are faced with constant increases in the cost of living and a decline in the purchasing power of the dollar.
There are two or three other changes I should like to have seen made in this resolution. I should have liked these proposals to have included a provision that all property taxes be deductible for income tax purposes. I read an article some time ago to the effect that the Progressive Conservative Party intended to make this one of the planks in its election platform. We are not surprised. It would not be the first time that they have taken planks out of our platform and used them. This is something we have advocated for a number of years. In fact I have a document here which was put out a long time ago by the Social Credit Association of Canada and on page 16 we read: "Full property taxes should be an allowable deduction for income tax purposes".

Income Tax Act
I have an article here from the Ottawa Citizen of May 20, 1965. I will read part of it. It says:
A resolution asking for some relief from personal income tax for homeowners was approved Wednesday by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities.
The mayors agreed at their annual meeting that the money paid out in municipal taxes should not be subject to further taxation and should be a deductible item on the income tax form.
Once again I am happy that Social Credit is right in line with popular proposals. I believe the Minister of Finance should take cognizance of this recommendation and have it included in the resolution, and in the bill which is to follow.
I do not expect it will have any practical result but I believe it does not hurt to reiterate some of these things. If the Minister of Finance wanted to find a way of helping the economy he could have done so by rescinding the legislation with regard to the taxes on building materials and production machinery. The Minister has insisted down through the months that this action was necessary and justified, but I suggest that in the over-all picture the rescinding of these taxes would have provided a tremendous boost to the economy.
Clause 10 of the resolution has to do with income tax allowances in respect of clearing land or laying tile drainage for the purpose of carrying on a farm business. This is a commendable provision. Possibly it will have a decided impact on the economy of various communities, especially in areas where it is necessary to do a great deal of land clearing and levelling in order to make farming profitable. We express appreciation to the Minister for this proposal at least.
I do not intend to take any further time dealing with this measure but we trust that the day is not too distant when the Minister of Finance, basing his considerations on the report of the Royal Commission, will work out some way of bringing to the people of Canada adequate and effective relief from the burden of taxation which is now becoming intolerable.

First, may I say that while we differ from the Minister strongly on certain questions relating to taxation, all of us in this group look upon him as one of the nicest men who ever undertook legally to pick a Canadian pocket.
We presume this is a stopgap budget, a mark-time budget, as it were. As the Minister has mentioned, the Government is await-

ing a report from the Royal Commission on Taxation. I hope that when we get this report it will provide an opportunity for us to lay a sound and equitable tax base in Canada. Positions with regard to Federal and Provincial taxation are changing. I do hope that as a result of this report the Provinces and the Federal Government will have an opportunity to develop a logical tax structure in which fields of taxation and responsibility are clearly defined.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
There is great concern among many people of this country about United States ownership and control of our resources and our industries, as well as concern about borrowings from the United States particularly by municipalities for the development of social projects in Canada. In that connection I should like to read an extract from a pamphlet sent to me by some students in Montreal. It is entitled "Identity". I have talked with a number of students in universities throughout this country and I have been very pleased to discover that there are large and increasing numbers of young people who are interested in the type of society we are developing under the present circumstances.
I feel that the following statement is rather good:
Again, if we desire an equalitarian society in Canada then we must have ownership and control of our economy. It is simply impossible to create a country with full medicare, full pensions, free education for everyone, full employment with a high degree of cultural leisure life, while the wealth we create fills the coffers of another country and our resources are utilized for that country's benefit.
In that connection all of us in this group wish the Minister every success in all he undertakes to restore Canadian ownership in those fields I mentioned previously.
It is my intention now to make a few observations in respect of exemptions. From my own personal experience I believe there are some valid reasons for suggesting that the exemption of expenses in respect of travellers and others entertaining in connection with business is sometimes overdone. I have actually been present when commercial travellers have phoned to points 100 miles from where they were taking orders, who in turn put in expenses as though they had travelled to the point to get the order in question. More attention should be paid in respect of these business expenses.
Recently I was in Montreal and received information to the effect that there are golf clubs there with membership fees of $5,000
June 15>
1365

per year. I was told by one of the members that the membership fee is deductible for income tax purposes because this was considered as a form of entertainment for customers and clients. This is another aspect of this question of deductible expenses that should be looked into very carefully.
One other matter I wish to mention, which has irritated me considerably because I am strongly opposed to this form of exemption, is the matter of exemptions allowed to the organization known as the Moral Re-Armament organization. I know that when I talk about this subject I tread on the toes of some very sincere and honest people, but I have gone into this question very thoroughly and I know of what I speak. I may say that I was told once by a former member of the Cabinet that in his opinion he considered this a most sinister organization.
This organization receives very large exemptions on the grounds that it is a religious and charitable organization. It carries on very expensive advertising in daily newspapers in Canada. It publishes books, and has other large expenses of a similar nature. When I asked a question in this vein I was told by the Minister that the reason for these exemptions was based on the fact that this organization is considered to be a religious, charitable body. Anyone who examines the records in the Companies Branch of the Department of Secretary of State will find some very interesting information-information that caused a Cabinet minister some years ago to say that he agreed with my standpoint in this regard, because in his opinion this was a very sinister organization, organized to promote the cold war. I think if the Minister looks into this matter he will find that the largest contributions to this organization are made by large segments of industry interested in defence production. This is a matter that should be investigated.
I do not intend to say anything more in this regard at this time, except that I hope these remarks will be considered by the Minister. Various trade unions in my constituency, members of political organizations to which I belong and members of other organizations, have asked me to bring this matter to the attention of the House under the appropriate item, and that is what I have done at this time, because they object to this Moral Re-Armament organization receiving large exemptions on the ground that it is a religious or charitable group. The activities of this organization warrant a much more thorough and complete investigation than has
Income Tax Act
been undertaken by the Minister of National Revenue or any official of the Government to date. This investigation should also relate to the source of this organization's funds and the purposes for which they are used. I am sure that anyone who knows the truth about this organization must realize that it is not a religious organization in the accepted sense of the word, and I would ask the Minister to inform us as to the basis on which it receives these large exemptions as being a charitable organization.
While we do allow exemptions to businesses, as I have mentioned, I think in many cases this involves an abuse. We allow exemptions to organizations such as the Moral Re-Armament group while at the same time we do not allow legitimate travelling expenses of individuals like many who live in my constituency, who have to travel 30 miles every day to their places of employment. I urge the Minister to give some consideration in this regard. Some consideration should be given to the living expenses of individuals who must maintain two homes because they are employed at logging and mining camps. There are no exemptions allowed under the existing system of taxation for these extra expenses. I think circumstances of this kind warrant further consideration by the Minister.
Having made these very mild criticisms I should now like to refer to paragraph 10 of the resolution. Subparagraph (b) of this paragraph relates to landscaping of property used by the taxpayer for the purpose of gaining or producing income. I think that is a pretty wide provision and, while as a Socialist I would expect all good capitalists of any size to be able to pay for this landscaping themselves, because of my love for beauty in all its forms, whether natural or otherwise, I would agree with this exemption with a certain amount of reservation.
Subparagraph (c) reads:
for clearing land or laying tile drainage for the purpose of carrying on a farming business,
I must say that I was very pleased indeed that the Minister included that exemption in his budget resolution. For 15 years I have risen in this House and argued that the farmer who brought land into production by clearing, by draining or by irrigation should be allowed the same exemption allowed to the owners of mines, or gas or oil wells. I am very pleased indeed that the Minister has included this exemption, and I know that the agricultural organizations in my constituency as well as the Canadian Federation of Agri-

June 15, 1965
Income Tax Act
culture, the Farmers Union and all those interested in developing agriculture and increasing production, will welcome this exemption, which is actually only the granting ol that justice to the agricultural industry which has been denied for so many years.
I should now like to refer to subclause (d) which reads-
-as or on account of the cost of making representations to a government, municipality or other public authority in connection with a business carried on by the taxpayer, including representations for the purpose of obtaining a licence, permit, franchise, or trade mark,
I support this exemption in principle, but I envisage the risk, if it is not carefully policed, that there will be abuses. I think individuals who come here as delegates representing various organizations should be allowed to deduct their legitimate expenses. In respect to those who incur expenses in making representation, I should like the Minister to inform me whether it would be possible for a Member of Parliament who is a lawyer, to make representations to the Government on behalf of a client, the charges for which would be exempted as income of that client under the provisions of this subsection. I am going to make a speech on this question a little later on a much broader scale. But while the principle that it will benefit agricultural organizations, trade unions, business organizations and others with a legitimate expense incurred in presenting their views to the Government is correct, there is the possibility of this principle being abused, if it is not carefully policed. Knowing that others wish to say a few words on this resolution I will bring my remarks to an end at this point, but I may take an opportunity at a later date to add a few brief words.
[DOT] (8:50 pjn.)

Mr. Chairman, in entering this debate it is not my purpose to hold up a decision on these resolutions, nor to repeat anything which has already been said. However, the last speaker raised a point about a certain organization, which I felt should not be allowed to go on the record unchallenged. I do not belong to this organization, nor do I hold any particular brief for it. I am referring to the remarks made by the last speaker about Moral Re-Armament.
He made certain allegations which would seem to disclose to this committee that in some way he obtained information from the Department of National Revenue about the source of income of this organization. As I
[Mr. Herridge.l
understand the Act the Department is not at liberty to disclose anyone's personal business in connection with donations that he may make, or that any company may make which are legitimate within the laws of the land. I challenge the hon. Member to produce evidence that what he stated-namely, that this organization is supported by munitions manufacturers and others-is indeed the fact.
Although I said, Mr. Chairman, that I was not connected in any way with this organization, I have had the opportunity to visit abroad various symposiums they have held and to meet and discuss problems with people from many countries of the world who have attended them. Although they still remain an enigma to me in many respects, and although for certain reasons I cannot directly join or support them, I still came away from these symposiums which I was privileged to attend with the feeling that this meeting together, and the influence the meetings had on the peoples from newly emerging countries, and others, were for the good.
I know that the hon. Member for Kootenay West and other Members of his group think that everyone should lie down and let Communism have full sway in this world; that it is not right to stand up and protect those things in which you believe. They say that we are the culprits in the cold war and that the other side is completely free from any blame. I do not accept this. The attack which the hon. Member just made on Moral Re-Armament, which I suggest is made without evidence, is similar to attacks which his group has been making on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Therefore I use this opportunity to bring this matter up, because I have not had a chance before to refer to these continuing attacks upon an organization which is without peer in the world. It is an organization which is almost completely unblemished. These attacks are bad for the country, and certainly do not help the morale of those in the organization, and their ability to do the job needed to be done in this country. In these attacks which are continually made, only one side of the story is given, and I am surprised that the Government and those responsible on that side of the House have not more vigorously refuted these allegations and stood up for this great organization.
Having said that, I want to refer to what I think is an omission in the resolutions now before the committee. Many exemptions are
June 15, 1965

made and, for certain groups of people, have been enlarged in some respects. I believe the Minister and former Ministers have had representations from a group of people who are not what I would call large wage earners in our society. This group of people are engaged in an industry which gives very little scope for individuals with their qualifications to operate, which means they cannot classify themselves as businessmen and make the deductions which a private business operation is able to make. I am referring to the mechanics who work in the motor trades.
The fact is that most of the qualified mechanics who work in the motor trades are hired at an hourly wage. To meet the requirements of the job they are required to provide their own tools. In this day of modern automobiles these tools have become very sophisticated and expensive. Sometimes they become broken and sometimes lost. Yet these people are denied by the Government in our tax structure any consideration by way of deductions either for replacement of tools or depreciation, and I think this is a real oversight. I should like the Minister to confirm that these people have made representations to him in this regard.
I recall that not long ago the logging industry received some consideration in respect of power tools used on the job. If this is the case, then I would suggest that these mechanics, who work in a very competitive market and who do not, in my estimation, receive too large a wage for the knowledge and skills they have to acquire, should also receive consideration. I say to the Minister that if it is too late to do anything about it now, I would appreciate some assurance that these people will receive consideration the next time around.

Mr. Chairman, as someone on the Opposition side may I say I appreciate the work which has been carried on by the Whip or his assistant on the Government side in arranging for a substantial number of Government Members to be in the Chamber since eight o'clock. Before I move an amendment I want to refer to one item in the resolution which has already been touched on by my colleague from Kootenay West, and that is paragraph 10 (d) which relates to the cost of making representations to the government being a deductible expense.
I think it is about time we had some kind of legislation relating to lobbies and the cost of lobbying. I think the Minister should tell us whether it is envisaged that a group like Dominion Brewers, who maintain an
Income Tax Act
office here and present reports at various times to the Government in connection with their operations, would qualify under this particular item. As I think everyone knows, lobbying on the federal scene is proliferating. I am not one of those who think it is something terrible, but it does seem to me that this particular item opens up all kinds of opportunities for underwriting the cost of lobbying. Therefore I think the Minister could tell us more about what is envisaged in paragraph 10 (d).
In connection with the Minister's remarks on budget night I want to draw his attention to a point which he made when he brought in the question of newspapers. He intended, or someone in the Government intended, to review the postal subsidy which, in effect, Time and Reader's Digest receive. All of us remember that last session the Postmaster General, the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, brought in a resolution to change the postal rate structure. As I remember that particular resolution it was not brought to fruition. A number of Members were against it, and one of the reasons was that which the Minister touched on, namely that we have no real idea of the scope and future prospects of the postal subsidy which certain publications in Canada have at the present time.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Since the Minister went to the trouble to refer to this in introducing the particular part of the legislation dealing with newspapers and periodicals, I think he or the Postmaster General is required by rules of fairness to tell us more of what is in the Government's mind. What does the Post Office Department know? I know the hon. Member for York-Humber was planning to speak on this matter, and he is one of the Canadian authorities on the question of postal subsidies and postal rates for newspapers and periodicals. From previous presentations he has made, I remember it is very clear that American periodicals coming into this country and the Canadian editions of Time and Reader's Digest have an effective subsidy that is not balanced in any effective way by any similar right that Canadian publications enjoy in the United States, because of a difference in the scale and the extent of publishing.
It seems to me it is not quite fair of the Minister of Finance to suggest that there may be some kind of adjustment here, when he is bringing in this resolution, that effectively naturalizes Time and Reader's Digest. I intend to move an amendment right after

June 15, 1965
Income Tax Act
reading a letter I have received from the Weekend, Magazine group, the group I referred to before as the main group lobbying against Time and Reader's Digest having Canadian status. I received this letter on May 4, 1965. It is signed by Mr. Mark Farrell, managing director of Weekend Magazine. He says in his letter:
For the first time, we are close in this country to an effective answer to the problems of Canadian publications. The policy on Canadian ownership announced in the budget speech is a sensible solution to what is obviously a sensitive problem.
Why, then, does the Government destroy the logic of its position by making an exception of Time and Reader's Digest? We might as well attempt to fight an outbreak of typhoid fever by making an exception of Typhoid Mary.
By granting these two foreign magazines special privileges the Government has cut the heart out of its own periodical policy. The facts about Time and Reader's Digest are well known. Both are American owned and American controlled. Both serve not Canadian interests but American interests. Neither in the true sense of the world, is published in this country; they are only manufactured here. Both are dumping operations. Both have a minimum of Canadian investment.
Not only are they unfair and ruinous competition, but they cost Canada millions of dollars each year. We pay them between one and one and a half million dollars in postal subsidies each year. We bonus them to the tune of more than $200,000 by exemptions from sales tax. We give them lower postal rates than many Canadian publications. We hand them, and propose to continue doing so forever, wholly unearned profits adjustable at will by their parents in New York.
Why? Justice certainly has nothing to do with it. The presence in a community of a social wrong has never justified its continued existence: Freedom of the press is not involved. Time and the Digest would be as free to circulate in this country as every other foreign magazine.
Whatever the reason, it is time we faced up to it. If a pair of foreign magazines can claw a place for themselves in this country in defiance of our own interests, we might as well give up. But why should we allow them to do so? As a Member of Parliament, the solution lies in your hands.
He is appealing to Members of Parliament. I am going to move an amendment to strike out all of subsection 2 in the proposed new section 12A found in paragraph 19 of the resolution. I move:
That the resolution be amended by deleting therefrom subsection 2 of the proposed new section 12A of the Income Tax Act as set out in paragraph 19 of the said resolution.
Before you put the amendment, Mr. Chairman, I should like to anticipate the objection that this amendment will disturb the balance of Ways and Means. Neither I nor the Minister of Finance can really give the answer or comment on that point. What the amendment does is to remove effectively the provision which gives an exemption to Time and Reader's Digest. I am quite prepared to ac-

knowledge that it may affect the two foreign owned newspapers to which the Minister referred either in his budget speech or last night, and it may affect a paper in the constituency of the hon. Member for Red Deer, the Red Deer Advocate. In other words, Mr. Chairman, this amendment deletes that part of the resolution which effectively naturalizes or Cana-dianizes Time and Reader's Digest for all time. I think the amendment should appeal to many supporters of the Government who I know have been concerned about this matter just as we must assume the Minister of Finance was last year.

Caucus rule.

Tell us your true views.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

You should respect the rules, too, you know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know them as well as you do.
I think perhaps I have made it clear that this amendment is obviously out of order. Income Tax Act
which I cannot give an answer, and neither can the Minister of Finance. This is simply a deletion. I should like to put it to you that if all we can do in terms of amending a resolution of this kind is to vote against a particular clause of a resolution, then we have not any function at all. If you cannot go so far as to delete something you consider obnoxious, then we have no function.
There is more to this particular item, Mr. Chairman, than the question of taxation, and the Minister is very much aware of it. This is a way of naturalizing something by a taxation mask or device.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the hon. Member arguing the point of order?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I am arguing against the interpretation advanced by the Minister of Finance in his comments on the point of order. He said that, in a sense, I had expressed doubt about the procedural legality of this move.
There is one other point I want to mention. The Minister made a personal aside. I should like to make the point to him that it is the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre who takes pride in being the procedural expert, and we take pride in that too. I do not know to what other hon. Member he was referring. I never claimed to be any procedural expert.
You have none over there, either.

It seems to me the point of order you must decide, Mr. Chairman, is not whether or not this amendment affects taxation revenue, whether up or down. It seems to me that cannot be determined by trying to interpret the effect of this deletion. I am arguing, Mr. Chairman, that you have to make up your mind as to whether a Member of the Opposition or any Member of the House has a right to make deletions from proposals or resolutions that come before us. I am not convinced by the arguments put forward by the Minister. I hope if you are going to decide you cannot put this particular amendment, that at least you will secure from someone on the Government side some argument a little more convincing than the one given to us by the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I say just a few words on the point of order? I freely admit that it is a difficult situation in which the Committee of Ways and Means

June 15, 1965
Income Tax Act
finds itself when we have a one-shot resolution with 18 or 20 parts. I also recognize the argument that private Members cannot move amendments that alter the balance of Ways and Means or appear to impose taxation. However, I should like to point out two things, and one has already been suggested, namely that we do not know whether or not the amendment will alter the balance of Ways and Means.
The other point I should like to make is that in this resolution, in paragraph 19, we have something put before us in rather unusual form. Usually income tax resolutions suggest in general language what is to be put in the actual amendments to the statutes. However, in this case there is set out in paragraph 19, not a general statement, but the precise wording that it is proposed to put in the bill that will be brought before us when this resolution passes. When we get to the bill itself, and in particular when we get into committee on the bill, we will be in a different situation. We will then have the individual clauses before us. At this point we have one resolution with 19 paragraphs. Because of a ruling that was made back in 1948, we are not allowed to vote on the individual paragraphs. When we get into Committee of the Whole on the bill itself, we will be entitled to vote on the individual sections as they come before us. If this section 12A is going to be written into the Income Tax Act as a clause in the bill, then we will be able to vote on that question by itself. As a matter of fact, when that clause is before us it is my view we will be able to move an amendment to delete any part of that clause. It strikes me it does not make sense to say at this stage that we cannot vote against a portion of what the Minister has placed before the Chamber, but that in Committee of the Whole, after second reading of the bill, we will be able to vote against a portion of what the Minister will place before us at that time. For this reason I suggest Your Honour ought to look more closely at the amendment.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
The hon. Member for Port Arthur has not moved any alternative. He has not proposed any form of words of his own. What he has proposed is a means whereby we can vote for a deletion of something the Minister has proposed, something we will be able to do later on when in Committee of the Whole on the bill, and I think we ought to have the same right now just by the rule of common sense.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure Your Honour is familiar with citation 263 (2) to which my hon. friend who has just spoken has not made any reference. It reads:
"The principle that the sanction of the Crown must be given to every grant of money drawn from the public revenue, applies equally to the taxation levied to provide that revenue. No motion can therefore be made to impose a tax, save by a Minister of the Crown-
This we all agree.
-unless such tax be in substitution, by way of equivalent, for taxation at that moment submitted to the consideration of Parliament;-
I should think this is the governing factor.
-nor can the amount of a tax proposed on behalf of the Crown be augmented, nor any alteration made in the area of imposition.
I suggest we are all familiar with attempts that have been made from time to time to eliminate a particular form of taxation. In the debate last Parliament, when an attempt was made to eliminate the excise tax on particular commodities, it was held to be outside the capacity of anyone but a Minister of the Crown to move such a motion. This clearly is a proposal for an alteration of a tax made in the area of imposition. For this reason I would submit to you, as has my colleague, the Minister of Finance, that this proposal is not within the capacity or authority of any Member to make.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The Chair wants to express its appreciation and gratitude to hon. Members, particularly to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, for their learned contributions to the point of order raised by the Minister of Finance. In the opinion of the Chair the amendment of the hon. Member for Port Arthur, if adopted, would have the effect of increasing the burden of taxation on certain taxpayers who otherwise would be entitled to certain deductions for income tax purposes.
I believe it is well known to hon. Members that when an amendment proposes to set aside a measure designed to provide relief, that amendment in effect imposes a tax and should not be accepted by the Chair. Citation 265 (1) of Beauchesne is relevant:
No Member other than a Minister of the Crown may introduce a Bill for the reduction of duties.
In the interpretation of the Chair this would be the effect of the amendment moved by the hon. Member for Port Arthur if it were accepted by the committee. The citation further reads:

June 15, 1965

The Government must take full responsibility for the taxation levied to provide the revenue.
I also refer the hon. Member to citation 269:
No augmentation of a tax or duty asked by the Crown can be proposed to the committee, nor tax imposed, save upon the motion of a Minister of the Crown-
I am not unaware of the difficulties raised by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre but I feel it is the duty of the Chair to be bound by the relevant citations, which in this case are 269 and 265(1) of Beauchesne. In the circumstances, with regret I cannot accept the amendment moved by the hon. Member for Port Arthur.

I am not going to argue with your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but I am going to make the point that there is something fundamentally underhanded and sneaky about the way this particular matter has been introduced into this question, because every Member knows that this is not a question of taxation. This has nothing to do with taxes.
Order.

This has to do with a fundamental matter in connection with two particular periodicals, something that spreads far beyond taxation. Hon. Members are shouting order. I do not know why they feel they have to substitute for you as a Chairman, but if they feel there is a point of order let them get up and say so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order please. I submit to the hon. Member that there is a point of order, that the Chair has given its interpretation of the amendment moved by the hon. Member and has ruled in the light of this interpretation. I would suggest to the hon. Member that he knows the ruling cannot be discussed.

I accept the ruling, but these remarks are for the benefit of the Minister of Finance, who was so kind as to tell us he was generally sympathetic, personally, with the intention that I may have had in mind in moving that particular amendment.
I am speaking generally now on something that has bothered a great many people in this country, and that happens to be the persuasive influence and the views of these two particular publications within this country, and their influence upon two successive governments. This is a very bothersome matter. I think most Members who feel the way I do, do not have any particular antagonism
Income Tax Act
toward Time and Reader's Digest as such, as magazines. In fact I would probably be one of the first to buy Time or Reader's Digest -Time at least-as an American edition coming into the country, such as the Saturday Review of Literature, Newsweek and magazines like that.
But this is a bogus situation. These are bogus Canadian magazines, and supporters of the Minister and the Government need to realize that what they are doing by supporting this resolution is Canadianizing bogus Canadian organizations. The point that Members who support the Government should consider, if they vote for this particular resolution, and particularly if they vote for this section of it when it is embodied in the bill, is that when they vote it will be for something introduced by a Minister of Finance who did not have the courage to come clear and clean and spell out Time and Reader's Digest.
This is a complicated resolution. It takes almost two pages in Votes and Proceedings to circle around the particular point of Time and Reader's Digest and to cover the rather simple point in connection with Canadian newspapers.
I hope other hon. Members feel what the hon. Member for Red Deer has felt, a sense of outrage that this Government and this Minister, after all the parading about Canadian nationalism, after all the talk they have given to us about being free, should stoop to this.
Hear, hear.

I wonder whether Members realize how easy it is to get sick of a Government that has a Prime Minister going around talking about the new politics, that has a Minister like the Minister of Forestry going around telling everybody to clean up, to get with the new times, to get with the new politics. I wonder whether hon. Members realize how easy it is to get sick of a Government which has a Minister of Finance setting forth policies in his budget speech and in his introduction to the Canada Development Corporation, about Canadianism and Canadian nationalism, and then see the Government come up with a device, a measure like this.
Cabinet Ministers will not even lay it out clear in the open. They are sneaking it through without even mentioning the names.
I think it is only right and proper that I, and other Members who feel strongly about this, should make the point, and make it

Income Tax Act
good and clear, particularly to those supporters of the Government who, in my mind at least, had given us hope that there was a real, genuine, pervasive Canadian nationalism on that side of the House.

I have some remarks to make along the lines of those made by the hon. Member for Regina City. They have to do
June 15, 1965

with mechanics and the fact that no depreciation allowance is made to them with respect to the tools they own. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I should like to say a few
words about the first paragraph concerning the income tax exemption currently being considered and made to apply as of July 1. The Government has suggested to the people of Canada that it is greatly concerned about poverty, and anticipates declaring a so-called war on poverty.

[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
Let us now consider paragraph No. 4 regarding the cancellation of the $500 tax exemption for individuals at age 65. This is another way of taking money away from those people at a time when they need it most, leaving them in a fixed income tax bracket, regardless of whether the extra income is derived from a private pension, an industrial pension or a professional pension to which the individual taxpayer had contributed.
The point I am making in this regard is, of course, an obvious one. At the same time the Government speaks of a war on poverty, by these provisions it is proposing a $600 per year benefit to individuals earning higher salaries and disregarding those people in lower income brackets. They are attempting to remove the tax exemption of $500 in respect of people age 65 and over. This will be a serious blow to those people, particularly in times of inflation, and there is an apparent trend of this kind. I think there is something wrong in the attitude of the Government in their projection of this measure, particularly
Income Tax Act
when one considers that they have refused on a number of occasions a request by Members of the Opposition to have old age security increased to $100 at age 65.
When we think of the Government giving this money to people in the higher income tax brackets and disallowing it to people at age 65, and when we think of the 11 per cent sales tax imposed on building materials, we are led to believe that the people of this country are being hoodwinked in regard to taxation. Mr. Chairman, in rising at this time to speak on the resolution I wish to direct my remarks particularly to clause 12A, which is that part of the resolution having to do with the newspaper and periodical industry. In commenting on this subject I should like to emphasize that this has been my life, and if I should be rejected in any
CMr. Fisher.j
future election I shall return to this business, about which I believe I know something. The hon. Member for Port Arthur was kind when he suggested that I was an authority in this field and I thank him for that reference, but let me say that I would not make that suggestion.
The question relating to Time magazine and Reader's Digest in this country is something which has received a great deal of attention, particularly since the O'Leary report was presented in 1961. However there are other facets of the game which should be considered before precipitate action is taken whereby naturalization is granted to these two magazines which have been established in this country, at least in the case of Time magazine, for about three years, particularly when one considers that it takes five years residence in Canada for a human being to become naturalized.
The interesting thing about foreign ownership of Canadian periodicals is this. I subscribe to at least ten foreign-owned magazines printed in Great Britain and the United States of America. I read the New Republic, of the United States, as well as the New Statesman and Nation of Great Britain regularly. I subscribe to United States periodicals, British publications, and to one French paper, and I have done so for many years. Is there something the matter with my reading a foreign-owned periodical when it comes into the country openly, when anyone can read it and know its contents?
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
It is stated that it would be bad for Canadian newspapers to be owned by foreigners. I am not going to argue the point one way or the other. But no matter who owns the paper, does not the reader of the periodical make his own judgment as to the ideas being advanced in the periodical? I have read magazines which have been published in Germany on technical aspects of the printing trade, and I think no less of them because they are owned and printed by a firm in Germany than I would of the finest printing trade publications printed in Canada or the United States of America. The fact that a publication may be foreign-owned is certainly nothing to be held against the publication, unless one is so weak-minded that he cannot form a conclusion of his own. The idea that you should not be able to read a newspaper printed in Canada which is owned by foreign interests runs counter to the fact that you can buy books printed in
June 15, 1965

Great Britain, printed in the United States, printed in Germany, printed in Australia, bring them into Canada and read them. Or are we soon to have laws which say that you cannot read books in Canada unless they have been printed in Canada? I hope we are not living in a hot-house economy in this held.
To grant naturalization to two United States-owned periodicals such as Time and Reader's Digest will be a body blow to the Canadian consumer magazine industry. At the present time those two magazines are taking from the advertising agencies and the few direct advertisers who are left, something over 54 per cent of the total amount spent on advertising in consumer magazines.
I am of an age that I can recall Canadian magazines which are no longer in business but have gone the way of all flesh, due to competition. I can remember the Canadian Courier. I remember when Saturday Night was a weekly publication. I remember when Maclean's magazine was a weekly publication. I can remember when the Montreal Standard was a great and strong publication under Lord Atholstan. Today the Montreal Standard is perpetuated in the form of Weekend, which is a gravure supplement appearing in a large number of Canadian newspapers. It is making a handsome profit on its present operation but has had to change its entire format to remain in business.
I can remember when Canadian Homes and Gardens was a separate magazine but could not meet the competition of those that the hon. Member for Port Arthur called bastard editions, if I may quote him; and if he is out of order we can both be ruled out of order. Now Canadian Homes and Gardens is a gravure supplement with the Southam chain. It is a pretty fine publication today, but it is not an independent magazine.
This question of allowing these bogus Canadian papers to continue on with the blessing of the Government has to be faced. Are we going to have a Canadian magazine industry, or are we going to have bogus publications dominating the field? The O'Leary Commission recommended that Time and Reader's Digest be taxed in a certain manner, one which would discourage advertisers from patronizing them. Senator O'Leary, who is a very much respected man in the publishing world, knows the business. At the time of the report he was President-Publisher of one of our great Canadian daily newspapers and familiar with the problems of publishing in this country. This is shown by
Income Tax Act
the fact that the owners of the periodical of which he was President-Publisher and chief shareholder found it advisable to sell the publication to a much stronger organization, F. P. Publications, who are turning out the paper today.
I do not know whether or not the Members of this House favour individual ownership of newspapers as compared with chain ownership. I personally favour individual ownership. But the competition which is arising in the magazine and publishing industry in this country is such that it almost appears that no one can stand on his own feet, even in the daily newspaper field in Canada unless he has chain support.
Reference has been made during this discussion to the Thomson chain. I have a brother working for the Thomson chain. Reference was made to the McGraw-Hill trade publications. I have a brother, now a naturalized United States citizen, who has been working for McGraw-Hill publications in New York since his graduation from the University of Toronto in 1948. Reference was made to the Toronto Star Weekly by some speakers today. I have a third brother who works for the Toronto Star Weekly.
Keeping it in the family.

I believe that with the connections I have in the publishing field I know all the facets of it viewed from any side. In answer to the hon. Member for Gaspe I might say that I even have a daughter who is at present working for the Toronto Star.
With regard to Time and Reader's Digest this is a problem which is faced by no other nation on earth. The United States of America is a nation whose people speak the English language, read the English language and are educated in the English language. In Canada there are 19 million people whose predominant language is English. The largest portion of the population reads English and the largest portion of magazines read are published in English. It is possible for publishers in the United States to try to invade the Canadian publishing market by issuing these bogus editions and soliciting advertising in Canada which is the lifeblood of the magazines. This is done, as far as the United States is concerned, in a foreign country. You do not run into a situation where publishers in France publish editions in Spain, or where publishers in Denmark publish editions in Germany, or where publishers in Sweden publish editions in Russia, because the editorial content of the French publication is in

a different language from that spoken in Spain, and so on. But here on the North American continent there is a publishing enigma which is not faced by any other two countries in the world, and so I believe a separate direct method of treatment is required to handle such a situation.
To allow the United States publications to come into Canada and solicit advertising without let or hindrance is a serious matter to Canadian publishers. We talk of the "brain drain" from Canada to the United States. I believe there are a large number of well educated and very capable people continuously emigrating to the United States, and I should like to illustrate how the term "brain drain" originated.

HEALTH AND WELFARE-ETOBICOKE, ONT.- TREATMENT BY DOCTOR OF NARCOTICS ADDICT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish tonight to raise the question of the treatment of narcotic addicts by doctors. I do so as the result of a report that appeared in a Toronto newspaper last week that a doctor in Etobicoke was being harassed by the chief of the Federal Narcotics Control Division of the Department of National Health and Welfare. An article in the Toronto Star of June 4 quotes the doctor as alleging that the chief of the Narcotics Control Division "is trying to interfere with anyone who treats narcotic addicts because he is afraid that we may show his department up".
The doctor referred to the fact that he has been treating a narcotics addict who has spent most of the last 20 years in jail for illegal possession of narcotics as well as for theft, in order that this addict may get the narcotics he required at a cost of about $100 a day. The doctor's statement has been confirmed in a letter to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) from the director of the Anglican Correctional Chaplaincy for the Diocese of Toronto, the Reverend S. G. West.
According to the doctor, this patient, one of a number whom the doctor has been treating, has been able to stay out of trouble to stay out of jail and to refrain from theft since he has been treated by him. The director of the Narcotics Control Division of the Department of National Health and Welfare has written to the doctor as follows:
The Department of Health and Welfare has no desire to interfere with medicine in the treatment of drug addiction so long as it is within the concept of good medical practice.
The Government and the Department talk frequently in another context about not interfering in the doctor-patient relationship, but there we have a classic example of Canadian practice in that the treatment for drug addiction is being decided, not by the doctor, not by the medical profession but in fact by the Government, by the enforcement officers of the Department along with representatives of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
June 15, 1965

This question was discussed in a recent issue of the Canadian Medical Association Journal and it was stated that it would be better and safer on the whole for doctors to stay away completely from treating addicts. What we are faced with in Canada is a policy which we do not admit exists because we have adopted the very pleasant and safe habit of ignoring all problems. The policy is that if you do not talk about these problems and sweep them under the rug people will be convinced they do not exist.
We have been following the same policy as the United States for the last 50 years in trying to deal with the problem of drug addiction. We have declared drug addiction to be a crime. We have followed the policy of believing that the crime can be eliminated or at least controlled by being ever harder, ever tougher on drug addicts, by watching them by keeping them under the closest surveillance by methods which can only be described as being part of a police state.
It is not my intention to discuss that aspect tonight. We can put the methods on the record on another occasion. This policy has been as complete a failure in Canada as has been a similar policy in the United States, in so far as reducing the number of addicts is concerned. Now, the medical profession, and this doctor in Etobicoke so far as I can find out, have been attempting to experiment with methods which have been used so successfully in Great Britain for a number of years. These methods have been described and explained in Canada by people in recent years, one of whom was Lady Franklin. I am suggesting to the Minister and to the department that they stop working so closely with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and stop following the police mentality and police methods. They should give the doctors a chance. They should give an opportunity to a few doctors in Canada who have not been harassed, who have not been browbeaten and who are not afraid to try this treatment. They should be given a chance to use medical methods of treatment. They should be given a year or two, whatever is required, so that they would be able to treat these persons as successfully as they have been treated in Great Britain. Then, we may well evolve a policy which may work, in contradistinction to the methods which we have used up until now and which have been a complete failure.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-ETOBICOKE, ONT.- TREATMENT BY DOCTOR OF NARCOTICS ADDICT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after the hon. Member raised this point I referred him to the position taken by the Department with respect to this Etobicoke doctor, and to the Department's feeling that any inference they were interfering with the right of a practitioner to carry on his practice was resented by them. They point out that, in the first place, the narcotics legislation was brought directly in line with the comparable British legislation as regards the right of a doctor to treat narcotics addicts and utilize narcotic drugs in such treatment. The hon. Member has just referred to the British system.
The department has been prepared to give full support to any doctor who undertakes the usually thankless task of treating drug addicts. At no time has the department sought to interfere with the doctor's efforts in this difficult area. The department added that the purpose of treatment in any medical sense is to lead to the reduction of an addict's daily drug requirements and eventually to his ability to abstain completely from reliance on drugs. They do not regard substantial increases in daily requirements as constituting treatment in any medical sense.
I suppose what drew the matter to the attention of the department in the present case was the substantial increases in the quantities of narcotics purchased by the doctor in question. He was asked for an explanation, as is provided under the authority of the legislation. When the explanation was given it became apparent that the daily requirements of the addicts under treatment were progressively increasing over a given period. In the case of one at least, the increase was six times the amount he was being given initially. This was drawn to the attention of the physician, with the suggestion that if he co-operated along the lines recommended by the Canadian Medical Association, there would be no further need to correspond, nor would any further difficulty occur. It is my understanding that the physician has agreed to do so. The physician himself has indicated that he will follow the suggestion of the Deputy Minister, Dr. Cameron and that he will work with these patients through the Alcoholism and Drug Addiction Research Foundation of Ontario. He is most happy to comply with that suggestion.
