ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-REVIEW OF CRIMINAL CODE PROVISIONS RESPECTING BAIL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I rise tonight to voice a plea for the very large number of Canadians who are grossly discriminated against and unjustifiably imprisoned when they are charged with offences and not permitted bail.
Last September 17 our Minister of Justice told me that he was preparing a review of the Criminal Code and that among the items under review would be the question of bail for those in custody. The other day, on June 14, I had thought that after nine months that would have been a sufficiently long time for him to have given birth to some new ideas in this field, and I questioned him about it. But in response to my question he informed me that the whole matter was now to be relinquished and assigned to the special committee.
My indignation was prompted by a series of articles by Martin Friedland, appearing in the Globe and Mail, in which he points out the very disturbing relationships between custody pending trial, and the outcome of the case, and the determination of the guilt, and the sentence imposed. For example he points out that 41 per cent of those in custody at trial were sent to jail as opposed to only 13 per cent of those released on bail. Some 79 per cent of those in custody received sentences of one month or more, while only 24 per cent of those allowed bail received such sentences. I have not time to go into the article more fully, but the point is that great injustice exists in Canada with respect to the whole question of bail.
When we raised this nine months ago with our Minister of Justice we thought we had a Minister of Justice who was going to take this matter seriously, who was going to speak out for the people for whom there is no voice, who was going to give some protection to these people for whom there is no one to speak. But we are fast learning that in our Minister of Justice we have a person who is long on promises and very short on performance.
He has had nine months in which to conduct his survey, to think about the rights of these accused people for whom there is no one to speak. He is the man to whom we look for guidance and leadership for these people, and from whom we have got nothing except this last promise, that the whole thing is to be
[Mr. Munro.l

swept under the rug and referred to this committee of experts.
I would have thought that at least out of some sense of humanity and justice he would have brought in some interim regulations which could be amended at a later date, but but that has not happened. These are our fellow citizens who are suffering this unjust discrimination. No doubt the Minister's apologist, the Parliamentary Secretary, will get up and fluff the whole thing off, just as the Minister has done himself.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-INQUIRY AS TO NATIONAL MEDICARE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I put a question on medicare to the Acting Prime Minister this afternoon. When the answer struck me as being not very satisfactory I suggested that it be posted for one of these overtime periods.
My question was prompted by the interesting announcement made this day, June 15, 1965, that we are going to have colour television in Canada in 1967. This was not only an interesting announcement; I am sure it will be very popular across the country. But it occurred to me immediately that if it is possible for the Government in 1965 to announce colour television some 21 months later it ought to be possible after all the years which have been spent studying the question of health insurance or medicare to make a similar announcement with respect to the intentions of the Government of Canada on this very important subject.
My question is a very simple one, a very narrow one. I did not enter into the whole subject of health insurance and I do not intend to do so tonight. It was this: Is it not possible for the Government some time this summer to make a clear announcement that it is intended to have medicare established in Canada by 1967, which happens to be our centennial year?
The Acting Prime Minister said my question would be given consideration. If by that
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion he meant that within the next few weeks the Government would consider the possibility of making an announcement parallel to the one which was made today, we in this corner of the House would be delighted. We are aware of the many years during which this matter has been under study, the many promises which have been made and all the election campaigns which have been conducted on this issue. Some of us are conscious of the reports which have been given us on this question-the voluminous report of a committee during the war years, for example. Then there was the Marsh report and the Green Books at the time of the Federal-Provincial Conference in 1945. There was the announcement made when we got hospital insurance that medicare, or health insurance as it was called then, was on the way. In the meantime many developments have taken place across the country. There is wide interest in the subject. Some of the provinces are now moving in a way which seems to some of us to be inadequate to meet the situation in accordance with recommendations of the kind made in the Hall report. We think it is a disservice to the people of Canada that this matter should be put off repeatedly.
The Liberals like to boast of the social legislation they have brought in during the years in which they have been in power. I suggest this is a piece of social legislation which should be put on our statute books. I ask the Government to subject itself to the discipline of making a statement as to its target date for medicare. I do not ask for a statement about the Government's interest in medicare and all it has done in the last 15 or 25 years. I simply ask that it give consideration to telling us before this House leaves for its summer recess, or, in the event that there is no recess, before this summer is over, that 1967 is the target year and that in 1967 we will get medicare. If this decision is put off again, year after year, we may have to wait a few more decades. We have waited 46 years already since the first promise of 1919. Surely that is long enough.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
Television itself came in only a decade or so ago, yet now we receive an announcement that within 18 or 20 months we can expect to have colour television. I think the Government ought to accept the responsibility for making up its mind that the next social advance to be made, and this would be appropriate for the centennial year, will
June 15. 1965

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion be a Canadian medicare plan. I would ask the Government to consider seriously the making of an announcement before this House rises for a summer recess, or before the summer is over, in the event we do not have a recess, that it has decided definitely that we will have medicare in Canada by 1967.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. C. Munro (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-INQUIRY AS TO NATIONAL MEDICARE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Speech from the Throne is in effect a Government announcement, or at least that is its purpose. In that speech it was stated:
My government believes that public policy should be directed to improving the quality of health services and to ensuring that all Canadians can obtain needed health care, irrespective of their ability to pay. Accordingly my government will at an early date meet with the governments of the provinces in order to discuss with them the way in which federal and provincial action can most effectively contribute to programs that will provide health services to Canadians on a comprehensive basis.
As the hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre already knows, a Dominion-Provincial Conference is to be held on June 19, and medicare is one of the items on that agenda. The Government has set out the principles it advocates in respect of medicare, and that it should be designed on a universal basis irrespective of the ability to pay. That is certainly an essential element of the recommendation contained in the Hall Commission report. The hon. Member also knows that the establishment of any medicare program requires the co-operation of the provinces, in view of the fact they have paramount jurisdiction in this field. Before any commitment as to a precise date can be made, discussions with the provincial authorities obtaining their feelings on the matter will have to take place. For those reasons it is impossible to predict the precise date of the adoption of a medicare plan.
The hon. Member suggests that such a plan should be put into effect by 1967. If we can obtain the agreement of the provinces so that the whole plan can be worked out in detail, with the implementation of certain of the Hall Commission recommendations, perhaps it can be implemented before that date. Surely the time factor must depend on successful conferences with the provinces, for the reasons I have suggested.
